talks.title: IT Ops Query: Ex-HashiCorp CEO's Startup Seeks '2.0 Moment' in AI Governance
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding IT Ops Query: Ex-HashiCorp CEO's Startup Seeks '2.0 Moment' in AI Governance.
talks.summary:
Overview: Former HashiCorp CEO Dave McDaniel discusses co-founding Dome Systems on the IT Ops Query podcast, focusing on AI agent governance after HashiCorp's $6.4 billion IBM acquisition.

Key Topics: The architectural shift from deterministic code to non-deterministic AI agent invocations; Dome's agent registry, MCP gateway, and LLM broker; and why AI governance requires new operational paradigms.

Technical Details: McDaniel explains that traditional software topology differs fundamentally from AI agents where a person calls code that calls a model with variable outputs. Dome provides centralized governance across this new topology.

Takeaways: AI agents represent a new architectural layer requiring dedicated governance infrastructure. Organizations need registries, gateways, and brokers to manage access and maintain operational control.

talks.title: The Future of Enterprise AI Agents: Governance, Security, & Scale
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The Future of Enterprise AI Agents: Governance, Security, & Scale.
talks.summary:
Enterprise AI Agent Platforms

Michael Clark of Google Cloud discusses building and governing enterprise AI agents on the Gemini enterprise agent platform. He traces his path from privacy and discriminative AI at Meta to agent infrastructure, viewing agents as integrating the full technology stack.

Interoperability and Openness

He argues interoperability, openness, and transparency are essential for agent ecosystems. Connections via MCP, agent-to-agent protocols, legacy APIs, and skills determine whether recursive, self-improving agents can integrate into business processes.

Platform Architecture

Google's platform spans the Agent Development Kit, hosting runtimes, context tools, and dedicated governance plus optimization and evaluation layers. The same infrastructure supports first-party Google products and external enterprise developers.

Consumer vs. Enterprise Governance

Consumer and enterprise products face different data obligations—regulations like GDPR versus internally defined risk tolerance—but both require similar governance concepts. Clark notes enterprise release cycles differ from consumer products because of compliance and accountability requirements.

talks.title: Enterprise Apps Unpacked: Harnessing AI To Combat AI-Driven Candidate Fraud
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Enterprise Apps Unpacked: Harnessing AI To Combat AI-Driven Candidate Fraud.
talks.summary:
Rising Candidate Fraud

Avature CEO Dmitri Boland tells Informa TechTarget that AI enables resume tailoring, application flooding, interview cheating, and impersonation—from unsophisticated ChatGPT use to state-actor remote hiring schemes.

Business and Security Risks

Hiring unqualified staff causes operational mistakes. Larger applicant pools also leak company technology stacks and processes to corporate spies, with North Korean remote-worker infiltration as a prominent threat.

HR Response Patterns

Customers serving banks, governments, and critical infrastructure see extensive fraud. Many shift administrative screening to AI so recruiters can meet candidates in person without ChatGPT assistance.

AI as Defender

Boland argues employers need AI scorecards and structured interviews to match candidate scale, detect inconsistencies, and separate authentic applicants from sophisticated infiltration attempts.

AI and partnerships

Roadmap mentions Agility Ops automation for infrastructure; industry gossip centered on Nvidia's reduced keynote/session presence despite Broadcom insisting the partnership continues and supporting Nemotron models.

Private cloud narrative

Broadcom leaders claim a private-cloud/AI tipping point and public cloud PTSD, but independent analysts and customer sessions still describe hybrid Azure Arc/on-prem plus public cloud—while conference mood improved versus prior post-acquisition angst despite smaller attendance.

talks.title: VMware Explore: Broadcom CPO Answers Private AI Questions
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in VMware Explore: Broadcom CPO Answers Private AI Questions.
talks.summary:
## Private AI Cloud Strategy

Broadcom CPO Paul Turner discusses VMware Cloud Foundation's private AI direction at VMware Explore with TechTarget's Beth Pariseau. Enterprises want AI workloads on infrastructure they control rather than solely on public hyperscalers, driven by data sovereignty, regulatory pressure, and cost predictability.

## Hardware and NVIDIA Partnership

Turner highlights certified hardware support including NVIDIA H100 and Grace Blackwell ARM CPUs, plus ConnectX-7 networking offloads developed jointly with NVIDIA. The AI factory concept runs on VCF-certified stacks, maintaining a close though evolving vendor relationship as product branding shifts under Broadcom.

## Sovereign and Regional Deployments

Customers across Europe, Asia-Pacific, and Canada increasingly demand sovereign cloud deployments where data and models remain in-country. Turner positions "private AI cloud" alongside existing private cloud services, expecting banks, telcos, and insurers to extend on-premises patterns to model training and inference.

## Platform Engineering Implications

The conversation frames AI as another workload atop unified virtualization and Kubernetes management rather than a separate silo. Organizations must balance GPU capacity, networking, and lifecycle management within existing VCF operational models while meeting emerging compliance expectations for sensitive training data.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Beth Pariseau from Informa TechTarget interviews Paul Turner, Chief Product Officer for Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) division, at VMware Explore in Las Vegas. Turner outlines Broadcom's strategic vision for "Private AI," detailing how enterprises can operationalize artificial intelligence infrastructure from bare metal up to production models within secure private cloud environments. The conversation addresses enterprise data sovereignty, cost predictability, network micro-segmentation, and the shift toward autonomous agentic workflows.

Key Topics:
- Private AI Cloud architecture: From bare metal infrastructure to deployed AI models
- VMware vDefend security extensions, distributed IDS/IPS, and micro-segmentation
- True Source open-source software vetting and platinum CNCF ecosystem collaboration
- AI "tokenomics", GPU capital efficiency, and transitioning to autonomous agent workflows

Technical Details:
Turner outlines the foundational architecture of the Private AI Cloud, which Broadcom conceptualizes as an enterprise "AI Factory." This full-stack infrastructure enables organizations to provision high-performance GPU compute clusters (partnering closely with Nvidia and AMD hardware) alongside virtualized storage and software-defined networking directly within their private data centers. By retaining model fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and inferencing on-premises, enterprises maintain strict data privacy and regulatory sovereignty over proprietary business data, eliminating the data leakage risks inherent in public multi-tenant hyperscaler AI endpoints.

To secure AI execution environments, Broadcom integrated advanced protections into its VMware vDefend platform. vDefend extends distributed intrusion detection and prevention systems (IDS/IPS) and granular network micro-segmentation directly around AI workload clusters, establishing robust East-West inspection perimeters to intercept lateral movement, prompt injection payloads, and unauthorized access to vector databases. Additionally, Turner highlights the True Source initiative, which provides enterprises with cryptographically verified, vulnerability-scanned builds of popular open-source databases and foundational components. Through platinum sponsorship of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), Broadcom ensures seamless integration with open-weight models and cloud-native toolchains.

The discussion also explores the operational economics of enterprise AI, termed "tokenomics." Turner explains that recurring public cloud API token fees quickly become unsustainable and unpredictable for high-throughput enterprise applications; running right-sized specialized models on dedicated on-premise GPU clusters allows CIOs to establish predictable capital and operational expenditure models. Looking forward to the VCF 9.0 platform release, Turner details the VMware Tanzu agentic control plane, which transitions administrative workflows from simple conversational chatbots to autonomous agents capable of dynamically orchestrating complex enterprise workflows across manufacturing, healthcare, and IT operations.

Key Takeaways:
Private AI architectures allow enterprises to harvest the benefits of generative AI and agentic automation while maintaining absolute control over sensitive intellectual property and compliance boundaries. Security leaders must wrap AI model runtimes and vector stores in micro-segmented perimeters using distributed IDS/IPS tooling to prevent lateral exploitation. Deploying domain-specific, right-sized models on dedicated private infrastructure provides superior cost predictability compared to the volatile tokenomics of public cloud LLM providers.

talks.title: Why NVIDIA’s Price Hike Could Hit Every IT Team
talks.teaser: Explains how a memory shortage and NVIDIA's price increases could raise IT costs for enterprises, even those not buying AI hardware.
talks.summary:
This episode of TechNews This Week, with TechTarget senior news writer Beth Pariseau, looks at recent NVIDIA headlines. The company's fiscal second-quarter revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year, with a 75% gross profit margin. Guidance points lower, to 74% next quarter and 71 to 72% in the fourth, driven by a global memory shortage fueled by AI infrastructure demand. NVIDIA confirmed price increases are coming, but did not confirm a report of rises above 15%.

The key takeaway concerns enterprise IT. Most enterprises do not buy rack-scale systems directly from NVIDIA, yet analysts say the cost still reaches them through cloud AI services and on-premises hardware, as hyperscalers pass on higher costs. Dell, Apple and Qualcomm have also flagged or raised prices tied to the memory shortage. Because most storage is now flash, long-held assumptions that storage is cheap may no longer hold.

The episode also covered an unconfirmed report that NVIDIA is in talks to buy Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. Hugging Face hosts many open-weight models enterprises use for governance and privacy reasons, so a deal could raise neutrality and control concerns. Pariseau advised IT leaders to focus on getting more efficiency from existing infrastructure, since the cost pressure may last.

talks.title: IT Ops Query: Exec Who Built Nvidia DGX Pivots to Sovereign AI
talks.teaser: Sovereign AI infrastructure, GPU access and the trust questions enterprise buyers should weigh.
talks.summary:
This podcast interview defines sovereign AI as infrastructure that serves a sovereign entity for AI development, national defense or public service. Stefan Fable, who previously ran NVIDIA's DGX cloud AI supercomputing service, argues the term is often used as a buzzword. He notes that data isolation, auditability and chain of custody also matter to regulated enterprises, and that GPU capacity is concentrated in very few hands.

On enterprise adoption, he does not see AI infrastructure moving back on premises at scale yet. Chip supply is hard to secure because of long lead times, and running GPU infrastructure at scale exceeds what many operations teams can handle, a skills gap he compares to the private cloud push about 15 years ago. He cites an MIT report finding that only 5% of AI initiatives reach production. Trust, he argues, comes from minimizing risk and from local workforce programs with vocational schools, and sovereign data centers are framed as AI training and innovation centers rather than data centers.

On efficiency, he says closed-loop glycol cooling beats air cooling, while immersion cooling trades density and financing for efficiency. Sovereign initiatives often require heterogeneous hardware, though NVIDIA still dominates. For enterprise buyers, the takeaway is to ask how much trust they are willing to extend to a provider, since fine-tuning models on sensitive data hands over highly confidential information.

talks.title: Targeting AI: Math Plus AI -- A Way To Control Agents
talks.teaser: Discusses a math-based approach to governing enterprise AI agents, with traceability and human control, and the debate over AGI.
talks.summary:
This podcast interview opens with the guest's enterprise AI company, which builds a platform to orchestrate AI agents across business functions such as supply chain, accounting, HR and compliance. The guest explains that the platform rests on mathematical foundations, including category theory, type theory and neuro-symbolic AI, rather than on pattern recognition alone. Instead of having agents pass information over ordinary communication channels, the design connects them through typed contracts, so errors can be contained, traced and audited.

The guest says this layer sits above whichever large language model a customer uses, so the platform stays model-agnostic. A meta agent inside the orchestrator is described as spotting errors that reach this layer, stopping them from spreading and correcting them over time. Healthcare and finance are named as target sectors, where doctors and regulators would need to trace decisions and test what-if alternatives. The guest repeatedly stresses that humans stay in control of the system.

Much of the discussion turns on trust. The host and guest compare agent deployment to building inspections and chip testing, arguing that enterprises are putting agents into production before verifying them. The guest also doubts that current language models will reach AGI, and contrasts the approach with world-model research. Autonomous driving is offered as an example of an AI stack that might reduce reliance on detailed maps. The takeaway is that governance and traceability need to be built in before agent deployments scale.

talks.title: Beyond Visibility: Decision Intelligence In the Supply Chain
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Beyond Visibility: Decision Intelligence In the Supply Chain.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Jett McCandless, CEO of Project 44, discusses how supply chain visibility has evolved from a competitive advantage to a baseline requirement, and how the industry must now shift focus toward decision intelligence and autonomous action. The podcast explores how organizations drowning in supply chain data can transform passive visibility into proactive, AI-driven decision-making.

## Key Topics
McCandless distinguishes between two types of visibility: "little v" (tracking shipments and ETAs) and "big V" (tracking POs and part numbers across supply chain nodes). While these visibility layers have matured, the real challenge is that supply chain managers are overwhelmed with alerts and dashboards but lack the ability to act decisively. The solution is decision intelligence—using AI agents to automatically recommend or execute actions like expediting orders, rerouting inventory, or adjusting promotional strategies.

## Project 44 Platform
Project 44 tracks 1.5 billion shipments annually across 267,000+ carriers in 190+ countries, with approximately $4 trillion in GDP flowing through the platform daily. The platform comprises four product families: an intelligent transportation management system, visibility layer, yard operations management, and last-mile e-commerce capabilities. The system processes roughly 8 billion events per day and maps the entire planet down to hexagonal grid squares to identify choke points and disruptions.

Data prioritization occurs through a three-step process: ingesting global events from social media, news, and logistics data; associating those events with shipments; and allowing customers to define what constitutes actionable exceptions for their specific business. This ensures alerts are contextual—an auto manufacturer's priorities differ from a life sciences company's, for example.

## Trust and Data Quality
McCandless emphasizes that AI-driven decisions are only trustworthy when built on high-fidelity data. Project 44 prioritizes direct carrier connectivity, ensuring access to each carrier's highest-quality data stream. The platform supplements carrier data with satellite imagery, highway cameras, agent-based inquiries, and comprehensive geographic mapping. Critically, the system is operator-controlled: customers toggle features on and off, start with specific geographies or transport modes, and review detailed logs of agent performance.

## Customer Evidence
Notable customers include Ford, BMW, Goodyear, Kellogg's, Amazon, Home Depot, and Costco. A public case study from El Con (life sciences) demonstrates nine-figure inventory savings through improved lead time visibility. Gartner data shows 21 of the top 25 supply chain professionals are Project 44 customers, and 9 of the top 10 logistics service providers use the platform. Every LSP that dropped out of the top 10 over the past decade was not a Project 44 customer; every company that rose into the top 10 was.

## Obstacles and Advice
The primary blocker to success is carrier connectivity and data quality—once achieved, it enables everything downstream. Change management is the secondary challenge, as organizations must rethink workflows and cross-enterprise collaboration. For companies beginning their journey, McCandless advises: define a North Star vision (e.g., direct-to-consumer sales), assess current capabilities and tech stack, identify quick wins achievable in 60–90 days, and avoid becoming dependent on large infrastructure projects like ERP migrations. Building early ROI creates budget and organizational credibility for sustained modernization.

talks.title: IT Ops Query: Red Hat's Lightwell Reflects New Agentic AI Security Urgency
talks.teaser: Explains how Red Hat's Lightwell service handles open source vulnerability patching as AI speeds up vulnerability discovery.
talks.summary:
The episode opens with the open-weight model debate, which Brian Gracely of Red Hat describes as a familiar technology transition complicated by geopolitical concerns about China. The discussion then turns to open source security. Gracely argues that AI tools have lowered the cost of finding vulnerabilities, while many enterprises run older Java, Linux and other software that they prefer not to upgrade because of large dependency trees.

He explains Lightwell, formerly Project Lightwell, which extends Red Hat's protection to Java and Python dependencies. Customers submit vulnerabilities their scans found in the specific older versions they want to keep. Red Hat fixes those versions, returns the fixes under an embargo window of about 14 days, and then passes them upstream to maintainers. Partners that provide network-level remediation help customers who cannot patch within that window. Customers have reported finding thousands of vulnerabilities at a time and want prioritization based on their own environment, not only CVSS scores.

On trust, Gracely says Red Hat aims for transparency, chain of trust and attestation, and asks customers to test fixes before putting them into production. For practitioners, he suggests measuring how long a patch takes to reach production, since delays beyond 14, 21 or 30 days point to technical debt in patching processes.

talks.title: Black Hat's Biggest Shift: AI Attacks Are Here, and Getting Smarter
talks.teaser: The episode recaps Black Hat trends on AI-driven attacks and the old threats that still persist.
talks.summary:
Sharon Shea, executive editor at TechTarget Cybersecurity, joins this episode of Tech News This Week to recap Black Hat, which she attended for the first time. She said the show came only weeks after a run of high-profile AI model incidents, so by the conference the mood had shifted from asking whether AI-driven attacks would happen to accepting that they are already here. Attendees focused on working together to understand what went wrong and how to fix it.

She described reports of automated AI-enabled attacks that were loud and noisy but not stealthy, often tripping over deception tools such as canaries and honeypots. A threat-hunting session covered what it called a first low-and-slow AI-enabled attack, allegedly carried out by a nation-state actor, which she framed as a preview of what is coming. On patching, she pointed to CISA guidance from June telling federal agencies to fix the highest-risk flaws first and defer lower-severity ones, and noted interest in virtual patching as a temporary fix. She also cited the attacks on US water and wastewater PLCs, low in complexity but exploiting internet-connected legacy devices that lack MFA and encryption.

Common strategy themes were familiar: complete asset visibility, access control with MFA and passkeys, least privilege and just-in-time access, zero trust, segmentation and security awareness training, alongside newer use of defense-focused AI models. Looking ahead, she said she will watch whether noisy AI attacks turn stealthy, how accountability for AI agents is assigned to a named owner, and how government involvement plays out, along with "harnesses," the controls placed around agents.

talks.title: Why EY built an entire AI platform for enterprise-scale agentic AI
talks.teaser: Explains how EY built a shared agentic AI platform, its three layers, and the data and trust lessons behind it.
talks.summary:
EY, a large professional services firm, found that its generative AI work had splintered into disconnected co-pilots, models and workflows as agentic AI arrived. Data sat across many systems, governance varied, and many pilots stalled before reaching enterprise scale. The firm set four goals: make data AI-ready and trusted, apply one governance model, and move from isolated use cases to enterprise-wide value. With Microsoft and Nvidia, it built a single agentic platform, with EY's role being to bring its partner ecosystem together.

The platform has three layers. A unified intelligence layer holds a model catalog and guardrails. An orchestration layer runs multi-agent workflows across email, documents and meetings. The data and trust foundation controls who can see which data. EY used the platform internally first, with 80% of its professionals using it and over 50,000 agents tested in nine months. Client examples included an SAP-based customer experience transformation and a shipbuilder where humanoid robots handled welding and painting under human supervision.

The guest argued that smaller firms need the same layers, since value lies between silos. The main lessons were that data matters more than the choice of model, that trust speeds adoption, and that leadership and change management decide whether people embrace the platform.

talks.title: Enterprise Apps Unpacked: Find One Strategic AI Use Case to Ease Pilot Chaos, Add Business Value
talks.teaser: Argues for choosing one high-impact AI use case, proving its value, and scaling from there rather than running scattered pilots.
talks.summary:
The podcast looks at why organizations struggle to scale AI beyond scattered pilots. The guest argues for choosing one high-impact use case, proving its value, and documenting the work before moving on. Pilots show a model can work but not that it pays off, and a single focus helps avoid sprawl by concentrating leadership, funding and data access. Candidates are judged by operational friction, clear economic value and readiness to change the workflow, with a success measure set first.

On execution, he says projects tend to fail when workflows are automated without being redesigned first, when data is not ready, and when executive ownership is unclear. In his view AI calls for an operating model change rather than a model rollout, run as a continuous loop tied to the chosen metric. Extending to later projects depends on carrying forward playbooks, governance, trust practices and human-in-the-loop design. A life sciences quality-control example showed that change management and staff reactions had been underplanned in the first project.

An internal example described employee survey free-text comments analysed alongside scores, with data deidentified, which surfaced patterns the numeric results had missed. He cautions that organizations often lead with the technology, when AI should serve a strategic outcome, and that fixed multi-year plans can give way to shorter planning cycles. The takeaway is to pick one measurable problem, redesign the process, document what happens, and then extend the approach.

talks.title: Enterprise Apps Unpacked: How One Manufacturer Blazed a Smooth Path to ERP Cloud Migration
talks.teaser: Follows a Quebec packaging maker's move from manual inventory to on-premises, then cloud, Epicor Kinetic ERP, with lessons learned.
talks.summary:
The episode is a podcast interview in which David Essex talks with David Paquette, director of technological innovation and procurement at Tilton Group, a Quebec City maker of thermoformed packaging. Before the ERP project, production was highly automated, but back-office inventory was updated by hand from production labels, which caused errors and required monthly counts. The company chose Epicor Kinetic after a benchmark study, went live on-premises in 2022, and ran a hybrid of classic and web screens before moving them over one at a time.

In May 2025 the company moved fully to multi-tenant SaaS Kinetic, keeping only a label-printing component on premises. Its custom manufacturing execution system stays on the shop floor for latency reasons and connects to the cloud through APIs built years earlier, so the switch mainly meant changing a URL. For forecasting, the company compared an in-house data science proposal with Epicor's IPNO module, which originated with a company called Smart, and chose the out-of-the-box tool as quicker and cheaper to deploy.

The speaker described a cultural shift toward data-driven decisions, near-perfect inventory with only a yearly count that corrected about 10 boxes, and better traceability for food customers. Pitfalls included carrying old customizations into the cloud, so he recommended cleaning them up first with Epicor's ERP Analyzer. Success factors included a long-weekend go-live, a test pick the next morning, and internal control queries checking data integrity, since the migration was not a simple lift and shift.

talks.title: How one manufacturer blazed a smooth path to ERP cloud migration
talks.teaser: A Quebec packaging maker describes Epicor Kinetic selection, SaaS migration in May 2025, MES API links, and AI inventory forecasting.
talks.summary:
The discussion frames cloud ERP moves as technically, culturally, and financially demanding, especially when multi-tenant SaaS replaces heavily customized on-premises systems. Tilton Group, a Quebec City thermoforming packaging firm, ran highly automated production but relied on manual, error-prone inventory and forecasting until it adopted Epicor Kinetic in 2022 after a long vendor selection and a COVID-delayed implementation with partner Groupe Concert.

The guest explains how “hybrid” meant mixing classic and web Epicor interfaces, then moving critical flows first to minimize user disruption. In May 2025 the company shifted fully to multi-tenant SaaS Kinetic while keeping a custom on-premises MES on the shop floor, connected through APIs planned from the initial project so only endpoints changed at cutover. Job schedules, bills of materials, and OEE data flow between systems; IP&O forecasting won over a bespoke data-science build after parallel proofs showed similar seasonality insights with faster integration.

Practitioners hear concrete outcomes: data-driven culture, annual instead of monthly physical counts with tiny variances, robot and MES connectivity, and continuous cloud upgrades. Pitfalls include pre-migration customization cleanup with Epicor’s analyzer, holiday-weekend go-lives with validation queries, and resisting lift-and-shift of unsupported customizations.

talks.title: Innovative reverse logistics app saves money while doing good
talks.teaser: Shows how Liquid Donate routes unsellable returns to vetted nonprofits, cutting retailer costs and automating donation paperwork.
talks.summary:
Reverse logistics, the process of moving returned or overstocked products back from customers, is costly and often ends with goods sitting in warehouses or going to landfill. Liquid Donate builds software that routes these unsellable items to nonprofits it has vetted. Donors cut shipping, receiving and storage costs and usually gain a tax deduction, while recipients receive goods they have said they need. Matching rules keep bulky items away from groups with little space and send clothing to organizations serving people experiencing homelessness.

CTO Aisha Azeez explained how the platform fits into existing systems. Rather than replacing e-commerce, returns and warehouse tools, Liquid Donate connects to them through APIs, and in one warehouse partnership it acts as the label generator. Nonprofit staff use a mobile app to check received items against the record and photograph them, and a donation receipt is then produced automatically. An AI image layer judges whether returned goods are still donatable, recyclable or fit for resale. Built Different, a t-shirt brand, saw shipping costs fall 20% to 26% on average, with some reductions reaching 80 or 90%, and shipping distance dropped by 1,300 miles on average.

The conversation closed with broader ideas. Azeez argued that AI speeds up coding but cannot replace engineering judgment, so newer developers should focus on system design, trade-offs and the reasons behind decisions. She also pointed to using return inventory data to reduce waste at its source, and to a restaurant food-donation concept as an area software could address next.

talks.title: The Future of AI Pricing: Outcomes-Based Models Explained
talks.teaser: The segment explains how vendors tie AI customer-service fees to resolved cases instead of token consumption.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with Salesforce adopting outcomes-based pricing for its customer service chatbot, contrasted with the usual pattern of cloud subscriptions plus AI tokens or credits passed through from frontier model providers. Customer service is framed as a natural fit because organizations already measure whether interactions are resolved successfully.

Reporting highlights how each vendor defines a billable resolution, with vendors retaining control over those rules. Salesforce bills when a customer confirms resolution or does not leave unresolved; escalation to a human is excluded. Zendesk uses a 72-hour quiet period before charging. Buyers and analysts describe confusion, unpredictability, and demand for caps, governance, and predictable monthly costs rather than usage spikes from autonomous agents.

The segment closes with pros—billing aligned to business outcomes and the shift away from per-seat models—and cons, including upstream model costs squeezing SaaS vendors. Practitioners are advised to negotiate clear resolution definitions, expect evolving terms, mix deterministic workflow with selective LLM use, and treat pricing as a moving market as more model providers compete.

talks.title: IT Ops Query: Block Broadens Goose's Loop with Builderbot for AI Agents
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding IT Ops Query: Block Broadens Goose's Loop with Builderbot for AI Agents.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Brad Axen, head of AI capabilities at Block, discusses Builderbot, an internally developed orchestration layer for coordinating AI agents at enterprise scale. Block, the fintech company behind Square, Cash App, Afterpay, Tidal, and Bitcoin projects, released Builderbot this month to handle the complexity of hundreds of millions of lines of code and hundreds of services. The project emerged from Block's experimentation with applying LLMs to real-world engineering challenges—enabling any engineer to contribute to unfamiliar systems and rapidly diagnosing and fixing production incidents before human intervention becomes necessary.

## Key Technical Components
Builderbot uses no custom model training; instead, it leverages frontier models and switches between them based on use case to optimize performance-cost tradeoffs. The core innovation is agentic search, moving beyond retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Traditional search algorithms failed; what works is a reusable capability layer embedded in the agent's tool-calling loop, allowing agents to detect failed searches and retry with different terms. The system is built entirely on MCP (Model Context Protocol), which Axen describes as "a service mesh but for agents," grounding the models through tools and significantly reducing hallucinations.

The architecture employs two types of loops: inner loops (the core agent loop where an LLM makes an inference, detects tool calls, executes them, and iterates) and outer loops (workflows involving humans or multiple LLMs). Incident response exemplifies outer-loop automation: a new problem triggers an agent to find the root cause, seeks human approval for fixes, then executes changes in another process.

## Performance & Results
Builderbot dramatically improves incident response metrics. Time to first response dropped from approximately 45 minutes (system-dependent) to 5 minutes, because AI can immediately check for potential problems. Time to remediation—how long to fully resolve and fix issues for customers—was cut in half, which significantly impacts customer experience. When tested against vendor end-to-end incident response solutions, Builderbot outperformed them because it knows Block's internal systems far better than any vendor could, enabling the agent to search relevant codebases and logs automatically.

## Quality Assurance & Limitations
The capabilities layer (tools) grounds models effectively. When agents use tools, hallucinations are rare; code understanding is "basically never wrong." Data understanding, however, remains at "medium quality." Models write correct SQL queries but struggle when multiple definitions exist for the same concept—for example, five different payment tables at Square. Block's pragmatic solution combines human review and an internal system called Query Expert, which remembers correct queries from domain authorities, creating a feedback loop to improve accuracy.

For code changes to important services, humans always review before production deployment. Similarly, analytical queries for high-stakes decisions (e.g., board presentations) receive human validation. Block has begun implementing AI reviewers for lower-risk tier-three services, allowing automatic deployment if the AI approves changes.

## Scaling to Larger Enterprises
Axen argues the value of AI agents grows for legacy systems with hundreds of millions of lines of code—precisely where traditional approaches fail. The barrier is largely organizational (compliance, SOC 2 requirements, procedures) rather than technical. Designers increasingly build functional prototypes directly in production systems, eliminating handoff delays. Multiple teams (sales, project management, customer support) now collaborate with AI from the outset, raising conversations to strategic questions rather than implementation details. Block generates a couple thousand internal prototypes monthly through this paradigm.

## Open Source Plans
Block will open source components of Builderbot: the desktop app (under a new name), the Slack integration, and possibly other parts, while keeping Block-specific MCP servers proprietary. Buzz, an AI-native communication platform similar to Slack/Discord but with integrated agent capabilities, is already open source (blockbuzz). The desktop app works with any MCP-based setup and appeals to both enterprise users and individual open-source developers.

## Broader Vision
Axen emphasizes collaboration across roles as central to enterprise AI's future. By bringing AI into conversations early—before lengthy back-and-forths—teams accelerate without replacing humans. Designers, engineers, sales, and operations work together in real-time, rapidly validating ideas and building higher-fidelity solutions. As models improve at spotting bugs (through patience and thoroughness), autonomous changes to lower-risk systems become viable, gradually scaling up as trust increases.

talks.title: Targeting AI: Rebellions vs. Nvidia: The Inference Chip Revolution
talks.teaser: A chip company's business leader explains its inference focus, open-source software, chiplet design and global push against Nvidia.
talks.summary:
This podcast interview with Marshall Choy, chief business officer at Rebellions, a South Korean maker of inference chips, starts with why the company concentrated on inference rather than model training. Choy says GPUs already handle most training well, while inference is where organisations put AI into production and earn a return on their investments. He also describes applications beyond text models, including agentic workflows, call-center systems, traffic monitoring in South Korea and medical imaging, all built around mixture-of-experts models.

The middle of the conversation covers business and technology. Choy outlines global expansion with legal entities in Japan, Saudi Arabia, Taiwan and the United States, and says the target customers are government bodies, neocloud providers, regulated industries and large enterprises. On software, he presents the company as an AI software business that happens to build hardware. Its stack relies on open-source components, and changes are contributed upstream rather than forked. The chip design uses chiplets that can come from several foundries, which he says shortens time to market and lowers cost. He also addresses competition with Nvidia, AMD and other startups, a merger with Sapion completed in December 2024, and a state-backed initiative in South Korea.

The closing segment looks at AI sovereignty, meaning owning infrastructure instead of renting it from cloud providers, and at the industry shift from counting model parameters to building infrastructure. The takeaway for practitioners is that open standards and transferable skills can lower the barrier to adopting specialised AI hardware.

talks.title: Agentic industrial AI and the indispensable connected worker
talks.teaser: Covers how agentic industrial AI turns plant insights into frontline action via knowledge graphs and connected worker workflows.
talks.summary:
The discussion contrasts decades of industrial AI centered on predictions, dashboards, and alerts with an execution-driven model where agentic tools help operators, maintenance staff, stores teams, and safety roles act on signals in real time. The guest argues the field remains in early innings: many organizations still invest heavily in insights while fewer than 20% of recommendations are routinely executed, and closing that gap demands operating-model change across OT, IT, and ERP—not technology alone.

Context layers built from historians, condition monitoring, process data, and enterprise records are framed as the foundation for trustworthy agents. The connected worker platform is described as a mobile, offline-capable system of execution linking SAP, Maximo, and OT sources such as historians, with persona-specific suites and emerging multi-agent flows that triage alarms and trigger inspections. Safety and operational risks—including permit errors and stale paper-based data—motivate strict human-in-the-loop guardrails and a staged maturity path before broader autonomy.

Customer outcomes in chemicals and specialty chemicals illustrate maintenance waste, faster emergency response, and reduced backlog when signals drive unified frontline work. The conversation closes with a five-year outlook: less obsession with insight dashboards, more semi-autonomous human–agent collaboration, and longer-term movement toward highly orchestrated plant operations where execution speed—not prediction alone—defines competitiveness.

talks.teaser: A Cisco data center executive covers enterprise AI infrastructure adoption, agent oversight, model costs, and automation tooling.
talks.summary:
Recorded at Cisco Live 2026, this interview opens with a partnership with Quali, whose stack automation tooling lets IT teams turn AI infrastructure deployments, such as an inferencing pod, into reusable runbooks rolled out at volume. Cisco's own tools handle day-two operations, including Intersight, Nexus Dashboard and its cloud control offerings.

On agentic operations, the guest said customers still want humans in the loop to validate what agents do, even though the tooling can automate the full loop. He described enterprise adoption as mixed: hyperscalers build their own systems, while longer-tail enterprises weigh return on investment. A central challenge is running compute, storage and several networks as one system, where a single wrong firmware version can take down a cluster. Asked about reliability, he said agent identity and drift detection tools are still early, and Cisco's agent studio pairs agents with security guardrails.

On cost, he expected workloads to be routed to models matched to the task, with frontier models reserved for critical work and small specialized models for simple functions. He named on-premises open-weight or fine-tuned small models as the best case over six months, and enterprises that cannot adopt AI and fall behind peers as the worst. For CIOs, he suggested finding concrete use cases, sizing infrastructure through t-shirt sizing, and building workflows with stack automation.

talks.title: Targeting AI: How humans and AI can co-exist productively in the workplace
talks.teaser: Explores how enterprises move AI agents from pilots into production while keeping humans in control of key decisions.
talks.summary:
In this Targeting AI podcast interview, AI Business hosts speak with Nikhil Krishnan, CTO at C3 AI, about putting AI agents to work in enterprises. He leads applied scientists who both invent new capabilities and deploy them at customer sites. The conversation turns to C3 Code, an agentic coding product that builds applications on the company's ontology layer, which he sets apart from general-purpose coding assistants.

On enterprise challenges, he argues that many AI projects stall between proof of concept and production, where data complexity, governance, security, accuracy and change management converge. He contrasts broad productivity tools with a small set of transformative use cases that drive most economic value. On data protection, he describes enterprise contracts that limit how models retain prompts, and an approach where most computation runs inside the customer's own data systems so that only metadata and queries pass through models. He cites one oil and gas deployment managing 8 trillion data points this way.

On work and ethics, he pictures the future of work as a pyramid: routine workflows automated, judgment-heavy workflows keeping humans in the loop, and complex operational decisions reserved for experts. His company avoids HR decisions such as hiring and firing, and checks models for hallucination, bias, drift and accuracy before and after deployment. Security, he says, rests on guardrails, supply chain tracking and full audit trails. The interview closes on the boom-versus-bubble question, where he argues that demand for concrete industrial AI use cases will persist.

talks.title: Enterprise Apps Unpacked: "Supermanagers" use AI to amplify human-centered leadership
talks.teaser: Explains how managers can use AI to support people-first leadership, team experimentation and skills-based learning.
talks.summary:
This episode introduces the "super manager," a human-centered leader who uses AI to help teams perform better without losing a people-first approach. Julia Buren, director of research at her firm, explains that the idea comes from a report arguing that managers are best placed to ease worker anxiety about AI. She describes the strain on managers, who face smaller staffs, frequent transformation and falling engagement, and the gap between what the technology can do and how quickly organizations adapt.

The discussion covers how super managers redesign work from the ground up, working with the people who understand each workflow and creating space for them to share ideas. Motivation comes from safe spaces for experimentation, hackathon-style events and AI usage set as expectations in goals. Examples include Car Gurus, which runs cross-functional AI workshops and coding weeks, and Microsoft, which ties responsible AI use to performance evaluations for employees and managers. Free Will is cited for its company-wide protoathon events, and a chemical company with 4,700 employees is described as building its AI transformation around growth and delivering value.

On training, the guest described continuous learning built into daily work and said only about 5% of organizations do this well. Managers can use listening platforms, AI coaches and skills data to act on employee feedback and place people in roles that fit their abilities. The closing advice is to make trust and transparency non-negotiable, give employees a voice in AI change, and remember that managers are employees who also need training and support.

talks.title: IT Ops Query: From Unix to NemoClaw, system design connects past to future
talks.teaser: Traces how Unix-style simple abstractions and kernel-level enforcement shape the security of AI agents like OpenClaw and NemoClaw.
talks.summary:
This interview looks at OpenClaw, an agent that drew attention in November 2025, and NVIDIA's NemoClaw, which followed in March 2026. The guest, a Carnegie Mellon computer science professor who co-founded Conviva, argues that both echo the Unix design of simple abstractions, where files stand in for devices, processes and directories. He describes the file system as a choke point where security policy can be enforced, and says NemoClaw enforces policy at the kernel level during runtime rather than only in a container layer.

He also discusses the limits of this model. Software bugs remain inevitable, and multi-agent systems combine probabilistic language models with deterministic tools, so the same input can produce different outputs. He argues that outcomes, user experience and security must be enforced and measured end to end, through continuous monitoring, detection, enforcement and optimization. He sees a tension between usability and default-deny policies, and separates personal agents, internal workflow agents and customer-facing brand agents, each with different requirements such as multi-tenancy and high concurrency for consumer-facing ones.

For enterprise IT leaders, his advice is to adopt agents quickly while getting the architecture and framework right, since a poor design becomes harder to run and secure over time. He notes that his company is putting together an end-to-end benchmark that it plans to open source for the wider community.

talks.title: What this week's Meta layoffs tell us about AI transformation progress
talks.teaser: Explores how recent tech layoffs connect to AI-driven role changes, over-hiring corrections, and workforce upskilling pressures.
talks.summary:
Meta’s announcement of roughly 8,000 layoffs anchors a wider 2026 pattern that also includes earlier cuts at Amazon, Salesforce, Oracle, Coinbase, and Cloudflare. The discussion separates headline blame on “AI strategy” from other drivers, including post-COVID right-sizing and ordinary cost pressure, while still treating workplace AI as a deeper shift than prior technology waves.

For large platforms especially, leadership messaging around agents, automation, and even manager-style AI tools sits alongside changing job design: some teams shrink specific functions while reassigning people to oversee agents or take on higher-level work. A software-testing example cited 40 manual testers replaced by automation, with many staff shifted rather than fully exited. Panelists also stress risks when entry-level coding and junior pathways erode, limiting future leadership depth unless companies acknowledge the disruption and employees invest in adaptability and soft skills.

Practitioners watching the market should expect uneven outcomes—expansion at firms using AI for amplification versus cuts where processes consolidate—and anticipate cultural friction, including morale hits and skepticism about “training your replacement.” The episode frames the moment as early-phase transformation rather than recession-style cuts, with broad role change likely still ahead.

talks.title: Targeting AI: Real-Time Intelligence in the Age of Generative AI with Dataminr
talks.teaser: Explores how a real-time alerting platform scaled from human review to AI-driven detection across modalities and industries.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens on Dataminr as a real-time intelligence platform that watches public signals worldwide and pushes client alerts within roughly 30 to 45 seconds. Coverage spans hundreds of event types, from natural disasters and politics to cyber and dark-web activity, for customers ranging from Fortune 500 firms and governments to first responders and newsrooms. The core tension is volume versus relevance: more sources reduce missed events, but filtering noise demands speed and judgment across text, image, video, and audio, often in messy or multilingual posts.

Joel Tetreault traces an arc from small source sets with human analysts on shift to automation begun around 2018, when scaling languages and modalities outran headcount. Early production models assisted reviewers; expert keystrokes and edits became training signal for geo, topic, entity, and caption tasks, forming a feedback loop akin to modern reinforcement learning from human feedback. Today models handle most alerts while people focus on edge cases and orchestration. The discussion covers chained model pipelines, preference for smaller fine-tuned models for latency and accuracy, multimodal parsing, synthetic data for new products, and curated historical alert data as a moat.

Later segments tie generative tooling and agentic workflows to richer context—what happened, why it matters, and what may come next—plus cyber alerting and the ThreatConnect acquisition relative to traditional security vendors. Takeaways for practitioners emphasize human-in-the-loop data collection, task-specific models over generic APIs when seconds and precision matter, and rigorous dataset design for global long-tail events.

talks.title: Enterprise Apps Unpacked: Using a citizen developer program to boost AI deployments
talks.teaser: Explains how a citizen developer program lets non-technical staff build AI agents, and how its value was tracked.
talks.summary:
This podcast interview with Fabian Cross, chief data and AI officer at a management consulting firm of about 200 staff, explains why the firm set up a citizen developer program. The guest describes three groups inside the company: technical staff who wanted tight central control, bold employees already testing consumer chatbots, and cautious colleagues who found the tools too complicated. Rather than centralizing AI work, the firm gave everyone a governed platform, coaching and a training track, while a small central team rebuilt a few high-use agents in-house.

Practical rules shaped the rollout. Staff could pick from several language models, with research tasks sent to a public tool and confidential work kept on an OpenAI model hosted on Azure. Nearly half of the staff were taking part, with 60 active builders at the time. Examples ranged from market survey drafting and statement-of-work drafting to roadshow planning and a checker that flags leftover client names and missing page numbers. Every use case required a business case, and actual usage was compared against projected value, with AI automation reported to have cut operating costs by 3%.

The main takeaway is that scaling AI is a people problem more than a tooling problem. Once a use case proved popular among peers, the firm moved it off the third-party platform and rebuilt it as a managed internal product with a roadmap, monitoring and an SLA. The guest also stressed that business users, not IT, should own usage and cost, and that a leader with hands-on AI experience should drive the effort.

talks.title: Using a citizen developer program to boost AI deployments
talks.teaser: Shows how a consulting firm let nearly half its staff build AI agents, with governance, training and cost tracking.
talks.summary:
The conversation covers a citizen developer program that a management consulting firm launched late last year so employees across departments could build their own AI agents instead of waiting on central IT. The guest, the firm's chief data and AI officer, explains that earlier centralized, ambitious projects went nowhere, and that staff fell into three groups: technical people who wanted control, eager users already experimenting with chatbots, and hesitant users who found technology intimidating. Nearly half of about 200 employees now take part, with around 60 actively building on a third-party drag-and-drop platform after an open-source option proved too costly to maintain.

Guardrails sit alongside that freedom. Users choose from several language models, using a research-focused one for non-confidential work and a hosted OpenAI model with company keys for sensitive material. Training is a short video course followed by hands-on exploration, plus weekly sharing sessions and a shared library of reusable components. Example agents draft market surveys and statements of work, screen contacts for roadshows, act as a personal calendar assistant, and catch leftover client names and page-number errors in slides. Popular agents are rebuilt in-house and run like products, with value tracked against business cases. The firm reports a 3% cut in operating costs and expects about a million dollars in savings.

The guest's main advice is that scaling AI is a people problem rather than a tooling problem. It recommends hiring someone with real hands-on AI experience to lead the effort, and letting business users show what works rather than chasing ambitious projects first.

talks.summary:
Beth Pariseau, a TechTarget journalist, joins the IT Ops Query podcast as a guest to preview Red Hat's announcements ahead of its Atlanta summit. She outlines four expected themes: private AI, sovereign AI, infrastructure automation, and AI operations with agentic automation.

On private AI, she explains that enterprises are growing concerned about the cost and control of AI development as token usage rises, so Red Hat is pushing OpenShift and its AI platform for internal model-as-a-service that lets developers test apps against models served in-house. On sovereignty, worries about geopolitical access drive interest in keeping monitoring data on premises, localized software updates and in-memory encryption in Red Hat Enterprise Linux. She notes that OpenShift underpins IBM's sovereign core product. On infrastructure, she describes hardened images that are not automatically pinned to the latest release, positioned against offerings from Docker and Chainguard, and a push into server virtualization with OpenShift virtualization as some customers leave VMware after Broadcom's licensing changes.

For agentic automation, she argues that reliability is the main open question, because AI output varies between runs and infrastructure provisioning needs consistent results. Her view is that Ansible could pair agent-generated infrastructure code with deterministic runbooks, and that users may increasingly reach such tools through agents instead of writing playbooks by hand. She closes by naming what she will watch at the show: real-world use of Ansible Lightspeed, how Red Hat keeps its independence under IBM, and how its tools will tie into IBM's HashiCorp and AIOps offerings.

talks.title: Enterprise Apps Unpacked: Understanding the science behind AI-based hiring assessments
talks.teaser: Shows how HireVue's Assessment Builder turns job requirements into validated assessments, and where AI fits in.
talks.summary:
This episode of Enterprise Apps Unpacked examines Assessment Builder, a HireVue tool that creates validated hiring assessments quickly. The host notes that assessments are often the most predictive step in hiring, but they have mostly been used for high-volume roles because building them takes so long. Mike Houdi, HireVue's chief science officer, describes the workflow: a hiring manager enters a job title or uploads a job description, the system maps the role to required skills, and it recommends a ranked set of assessments based on predictive power and fairness. The manager can then adjust the recommendations before publishing.

The discussion turns to how users control AI. Customers can switch AI-scored components on or off, for example using manual scoring for senior roles, and the recommendations stay effective either way. Houdi says the main trade-off is time, since humans must score interviews themselves. He also covers bias safeguards, including the removal of facial analysis in early 2020 because it added no predictive value, plus validation before release and ongoing testing with clients.

On the science, Houdi explains that industrial-organizational psychology underpins the tools, with over a thousand validation studies linking assessment results to post-hire outcomes. He argues that resumes and unstructured interviews have weak predictive value, so structured, AI-assisted evaluation can be both more accurate and fairer. The episode closes with planned features, including conversational assessments with AI personas and AI-driven follow-up questions for asynchronous interviews. The main takeaway is that validated, structured assessment is presented as a stronger baseline than resumes, though these claims come from the vendor.

talks.title: Targeting AI: LinkedIn’s Change to its Engine Could Affect Your Job Search
talks.teaser: A LinkedIn engineer explains how large language models reshaped job matching, job alerts and policy controls on the platform.
talks.summary:
The conversation covers how LinkedIn rebuilt its job search around large language models instead of keyword matching and fixed skill taxonomies. Caleb Johnson, a principal staff software engineer at the company, explains that older systems struggled with unusual phrasing and needed constant taxonomy updates. The new approach lets product managers write policy in plain English, and the system can explain why a job appears, such as a profile gap or a missing skill.

On the engineering side, he describes a teacher-and-student setup. A large model produces reasoning traces on whether a member fits a role, human experts grade those outputs, and the labels train a smaller open-source model that runs at scale. Job alerts now go out only above a minimum match bar, which cut unwanted notifications without hurting the business metrics he tracks. Bias checks run across personas, and a background pipeline evaluates production data for drift and hallucinations.

For employers, he says complete job posts with real salary, responsibilities and qualifications match better, and paying cannot buy a top spot. He also covers agentic tools: AI speeds up internal coding and a LinkedIn hiring agent helps recruiters, while mass automated applications and agent security risks remain concerns. Privacy is handled through a compliance layer in the data stack, and low-value AI-generated posts are downranked. The main takeaway is that trust and long-term policy should shape how AI is deployed in search.

talks.title: Google Cloud Next 2026: Breaking News on the Future of AI Agents, Cloud Innovation
talks.teaser: Breaks down Google Cloud's Next announcements on AI agent platforms, TPUs, cross-cloud data and agent security.
talks.summary:
This news segment was recorded at Google Cloud Next in Las Vegas. The host speaks with senior news writer Beth Pariseau about the conference's biggest headline, an evolution of Google's Vertex AI model development platform into a new enterprise agent platform. According to the discussion, it combines model garden, model evaluation and developer tools with a low-code agent builder, agent orchestration, an agent registry, agent identity management, an agent gateway and agent observability. Other announcements mentioned include a new generation of Google's TPU chips, a cross-cloud data lakehouse under an agentic data cloud banner, and AI security and governance updates, including integrations with Wiz.

The conversation places Google among the large cloud vendors. Pariseau describes its full stack, from chips and networking to storage and workspace software, and compares it with Microsoft's Agent 365 platform and ServiceNow's autonomous workforce offering. She says she has not yet found a clear point of differentiation against Microsoft. She argues that customers already invested in Google Cloud are the most likely to welcome the context, data and governance features that agents need to work reliably in an enterprise. The pair also note the move from assistants to long-running agents, and observability that tracks agent behavior rather than only whether systems are up.

Looking ahead, Pariseau expects enterprises to run agents from many vendors in hybrid, multi-cloud setups. She points to an open-source interconnect format released by Google and AWS, and to the cross-cloud lakehouse, as signs that rival vendors are cooperating. She plans to watch the TPU roadmap sessions and how TPUs compare with Nvidia GPUs on pricing and customer choice. The segment's takeaway for practitioners is to check how far customers have moved agents into production and how much autonomy they grant them.

talks.title: Targeting AI: AI PCs and chips in the enterprise
talks.teaser: Explains how NPU-equipped AI PCs run models locally and what they mean for enterprise productivity and data protection.
talks.summary:
Michael Nordquist, corporate VP of product marketing at AMD, joins a Targeting AI podcast episode to discuss how AI PCs and chips are changing enterprise computing. He describes the market as early, with use cases differing across commercial, consumer and gaming segments. He also outlines AMD's position across data center accelerators, servers, edge devices and PCs, linked by a shared software stack that carries from the cloud down to the endpoint.

He explains that AI PCs add a neural processing unit alongside the CPU and GPU, handling neural network workloads at low power. Examples include summarizing recalled activity on the device, live translation and transcription in Teams, and on-device image editing. On security, he points to virtualization-based protection, memory encryption against cold boot attacks, and a multi-year roadmap that includes stronger post-quantum key handling. He argues that keeping data on the device can lower risk compared with spreading it across cloud services.

On adoption, he suggests that refresh cycles could shorten if AI tools solve concrete problems for employees and for IT operations, such as spotting endpoint issues before users call in. He expects hybrid cloud and local AI to coexist, and treats separating personal identity from company data on agent-driven devices as an unsolved problem. His practical takeaway is that organizations should adopt AI PCs step by step rather than wait for a perfect generation.

talks.title: Targeting AI: The Agentic AI Foundation and Linux Foundation on agentic AI
talks.teaser: Foundation leaders explain why neutral standards for agent protocols and payments matter as agentic AI moves to production.
talks.summary:
The interview opens with the launch of the X402 foundation under the Linux Foundation, an effort that began when Coinbase asked for its payment standard to sit in a neutral home. Financial firms and large technology companies, including American Express, Visa, Google, Microsoft and Stripe, have joined its board. The guests describe agent payments as a coming step beyond today's focus on retrieving information and tools, requiring protocols for settlement and for setting the guardrails a client provides when a transaction takes place.

The discussion then turns to why the Agentic AI Foundation exists. The guests compare the move from experimentation to production in cloud and networking, arguing that agent protocols now need shared standards, coordination, security and auditability. On MCP, they push back on reports of its decline, pointing to strong SDK download figures and predicting that people will eventually stop discussing MCP as a separate topic, much as they no longer discuss HTTP. Openness is treated as a spectrum, from open-weight models and shared data sets such as Overture Maps to provenance work like the C2PA content authenticity standard aimed at deepfakes.

In closing, the guests turn to developers, whose work they say is shifting from writing code toward architecture, guardrails and security decisions. They warn that faster development also helps attackers find vulnerabilities, so maintainers of critical open source projects need AI tools to keep pace. A $12.5 million fund backed by OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Amazon and Google was described as a way to equip those core maintainers. The guests remain cautiously optimistic about where the ecosystem is heading.

talks.title: IT Ops Query: AI pilot to (Microsoft) Copilot: the state of enterprise AI
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for IT Ops Query: AI pilot to (Microsoft) Copilot: the state of enterprise AI.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this episode of *IT Ops Query*, host Beth Pariso speaks with Aaron Rich, Chief Technology and Innovation Officer at Avanade, about the current state of enterprise generative AI adoption. While consumer tools have achieved rapid adoption, enterprise adoption remains largely at an inflection point dominated by pilots and proof of concepts. Rich discusses the cultural, operational, and technical challenges businesses encounter as they transition from individual productivity tools to deep business process reinvention.

### Key Topics
- **Current Adoption State:** Most enterprises are still running experiments and pilots. While "AI on the business" (productivity aids like Microsoft Copilot) is broadly in production, "AI in the business" (core process transformation) is ramping up much more slowly.
- **Human Factors and Culture:** Within organizations—including tech-forward consulting firms like Avanade—employees fall into three categories: enthusiastic early adopters, an anxious middle trying to balance new tools with daily delivery pressures, and a reluctant group adhering to legacy workflows. Cognitive fatigue and the mental overhead of navigating approved tools and data policies contribute to hesitation.
- **Enterprise AI vs. Consumer Pace:** Consumer tools iterate rapidly, but enterprises require rigorous evaluation of data privacy, administrative controls, and compliance before operationalizing new technologies.
- **Workforce Impact and Digital Labor:** Rather than a direct one-to-one replacement of human workers, enterprise AI acts as supplemental "digital labor" (such as always-on assistants for project management). While labor displacement and role evolution will occur, engineering and core business functions are expected to adapt rather than disappear entirely.

### Technical Details
- **Data Governance and Security:** Enterprises face operational hurdles regarding data loss protection (DLP), access boundaries, and privilege escalation. When users build or publish autonomous agents, systems must ensure recipients execute within their own permission levels rather than inheriting the creator's elevated privileges.
- **IT vs. Non-IT Developed Agents:** Organizations are grappling with governance models for citizen-built (non-IT) agents versus centralized IT implementations.
- **Multi-Model Orchestration:** Platforms like Microsoft Copilot Cowork are exploring configurations where models (such as OpenAI and Anthropic's Claude) interact prior to serving responses to users to improve output quality and mitigate hallucinations.
- **Agent Orchestration and Cost Control:** Key emerging architectural best practices include establishing catalogs to promote agent and component reuse, preventing redundant builds, and setting up monitoring and throttling mechanisms to manage infrastructure consumption and model inference costs.

### Takeaways
- **Interdisciplinary Governance:** Effective AI rollout requires breaking down operational silos by running joint governance workshops involving data, security, and legal teams to adapt existing policies rather than attempting to rewrite them from scratch.
- **Targeting High-Impact Workflows:** Successful transformations focus on bottleneck processes that drive growth rather than just marginal efficiency. For instance, redesigning an end-to-end quote generation workflow by combining human oversight, traditional predictive machine learning models, and generative AI agents.
- **Outlook:** Meaningful transformation will take time; adoption is predicted to remain mostly in pilot phases through 2026 (reaching perhaps 35% in production) before seeing larger-scale enterprise production swings around 2027. Major risks that could slow progress include potential enterprise security breaches and behavioral friction.

talks.title: Inside SAP R&D on the convergence of agentic and physical AI
talks.teaser: Maps where physical AI is reaching enterprise warehouses and field operations, and what businesses should prepare for.
talks.summary:
This Enterprise Apps Unpacked episode features Yad Oren, who leads research and innovation at SAP. Physical AI gives machines the ability to sense their surroundings and act on them, as in factory robots, drones and self-driving cars. Oren argues that large language models let robots take plain-language instructions and handle more tasks, while work on perception, world models and safety, such as geofencing, is new to physical systems.

Oren's central point is that software will move physical AI from pilots into core operations, with 2026 as a likely turning point. The strongest demand he described is in warehouse management, such as pick and place and sorting defective goods, followed by inspection and field technician work. He also cited smaller models that need less compute and agent orchestration that lets robots coordinate with one another. SAP does not build robots; it offers a software layer that onboards robots from multiple vendors and adds auditing, governance and fleet health analytics.

Oren named physical security, data privacy around robot image recognition, skills gaps and regulation as concerns. His strongest warning was that doing nothing is the biggest risk, so organizations should imagine concrete scenarios with clear business value and start with small proof-of-concept pilots.

talks.title: Targeting AI: Navigating the AI landscape with HP
talks.teaser: Explores how HP sees on-device AI, workforce telemetry and ROI shaping enterprise AI adoption, from a company president's view.
talks.summary:
In an interview on a video show about AI in business, HP's president compared how consumers and enterprises adopt AI. He argued consumers move faster because they already carry powerful devices, while companies are limited to approved tools and hardware. HP's view of edge AI centers on laptops with enough memory to run open, quantized models of up to about 70 billion parameters locally, which he said mainly offers privacy, security and offline access. The clearest edge case he gave was retail point-of-sale systems and in-store analytics such as theft detection and shelf monitoring.

On adoption, he said customers usually get comfortable through proof-of-concept work and an ROI case. He described device refresh cycles that replace hardware every three to four years whether or not it is needed, and said a platform using telemetry from devices across vendors can match hardware to each user's role, which can lower spending and extend device life. He framed ROI as productivity, waste reduction or lower cost, depending on what a CIO wants. Asked about chip partners such as Intel and Nvidia, he said buyers care more about total cost of ownership and the work a device enables than the chip brand.

Looking ahead, he said HP is still known as a hardware company but is building a platform that bundles hardware, software and services for workforce management. His advice to enterprises was to avoid chasing AI out of fear of missing out. Teams should first define the workflow problem they want to solve, then decide whether AI improves it, rather than inventing a problem that AI can then solve.

talks.title: Plan a multi-agent orchestration framework for scalable AI
talks.teaser: Explains how enterprise teams can build a framework to coordinate many AI agents across security, policy and observability.
talks.summary:
This podcast episode looks at how multi-agent orchestration could change enterprise applications such as ERP and CRM. The guest, Peter Hess, argues that software will shift away from screens and user journeys toward services and APIs that agents call, with people setting goals and watching progress. He expects longer-term gains in productivity and reliability, while acknowledging that some short-term claims are overstated.

The middle of the discussion covers the building blocks of a framework. Hess lists an agent registry, secure agent-to-agent communication, a policy enforcement layer, centralized logging and monitoring, and an orchestration engine that stops many agents from overloading one shared API. Policy as code routes every agent action through a single engine, so a change to a rule such as GDPR needs updating in only one place. For traceability, he describes centralized logs with trace IDs and synchronized time. He notes that some models remain black boxes, so behavior is judged by watching for divergence from expected patterns. He also warns that tightly coupled agents can cause resource contention and cascading errors, and recommends looser coupling and explicit data contracts.

For adoption, he advises starting with one narrow, high-value use case, keeping a human in the loop for critical decisions, and expanding step by step. He points to open-source and commercial tools and to emerging standards such as A2A and MCP, and says integrators can tailor frameworks to a customer's compliance needs. The episode closes with his view that a double bottom line approach still serves shareholders by widening what counts as value.

talks.title: Mainframe modernization: Where AI wins and fails
talks.teaser: Explains why AI speeds up mainframe modernization only when paired with deterministic reverse engineering of legacy code.
talks.summary:
Asa Kellade, who works on migration and modernization services at AWS, discusses where AI helps with mainframe modernization and where it falls short. The guest explains that decades-old COBOL applications are large, mix several languages and job control code, and have little documentation, which makes them hard for a language model to interpret on its own. Deterministic reverse engineering is needed first to capture the code structure, platform-specific behavior and business rules, so that the old system's logic can be carried into the new one with traceability for regulated industries.

The conversation then covers the approach used in AWS Transform. Specialized software agents extract batch and transactional processes, data dependencies and existing documentation into a context graph. From that graph, specifications are generated and AI agents write the new application, with humans validating the output and checkpoints in place. Kellade cited customers such as BMW that have moved some components into production, with test generation and validation named as a notable source of speed-up. The discussion also covers hybrid setups where some workloads stay on premises, the parallel-run period when old and new systems operate together, and the continuing role of mainframe experts in these projects.

Toward the end, the talk turns to data migration, the shortage of new COBOL developers, and extending the same pattern to Windows and VMware estates. AI-assisted wave planning can factor in business constraints such as licensing, and continuous upgrades can address technical debt in Java and AWS SDK versions. The main takeaway for practitioners is that AI accelerates modernization most when it is grounded in verified facts about the existing system.

talks.title: SaaS isn't dying, it's changing: How vendors & users are responding to agentic AI
talks.teaser: Weighs whether AI agents will displace SaaS vendors, covering maintenance, security and earlier tech cycles.
talks.summary:
A podcast conversation between two TechTarget journalists examines whether AI agents will displace software as a service vendors. The speakers argue that the widely predicted collapse has not happened: vendors remain, but how companies build and host software is changing. Early-year stock losses are described as a financial reaction to a technical shift that is easy to overstate.

Examples include a fintech firm that rolled out an internal agent framework to its workforce, letting staff segment 100,000 sales leads in an hour. A separate engineer built an app that helped identify $10,000 in savings from a $30,000 monthly bill for one AWS service. The speakers say firms with strong in-house engineering can absorb more work themselves, yet systems of record such as CRMs still need long-term maintenance, governance and auditability, so many companies keep relying on vendors. One consulting firm hosts citizen developers' projects on a vendor platform so its engineering team is not swamped.

On history, a CTO argued this resembles the customized packaged software of the pre-SaaS era, with computing cycling between centralization and decentralization. Agents make customization easier, so smaller vendors are appearing to host agent infrastructure. The advice was to experiment aggressively in sandboxes, stay agile across language models, and choose between a vendor's agent tool and a self-built one by use case. The closing caution is against hype, since AI may not produce perfect systems from imperfect human-generated data.
