talks.title: Targeting AI: Understanding Human Impact and Safety in AI
talks.teaser: Examines how enterprises can weigh AI's human safety impact, covering regional rules, bias testing, vendor choice and accountability.
talks.summary:
This interview, recorded at a Gartner data and analytics summit, features Christopher Campbell, who leads AI governance and product security at Lenovo. He says many organizations are struggling to grasp AI's human impact, including effects on physical and mental health, beyond toxic output, hallucinations and bias. His team also looks at how a system affects local culture and society, since that shapes both project success and user trust.

On regulation, Lenovo's responsible AI framework starts from the strictest EU AI Act requirements, then scales to each region. A Japan example shows that a factory fatigue-monitoring use case the EU would prohibit may still be workable when governance matches its societal impact. For bias, testing covers languages and generational slang, and older model versions can carry legacy errors forward. Hybrid AI testing begins on local models and widens to cloud models to check for consistent results, while endpoint monitoring and a traceability effort help find shadow AI.

The talk closes on accountability: leadership stays responsible for AI incidents even when a model comes from a third party, especially after in-house tuning. That pushes Lenovo to choose vendors with aligned safety philosophies. For enterprises just starting, his advice is to ask vendors the same governance questions, build employee readiness, and avoid a one-size-fits-all approach.

talks.title: Direct materials sourcing technology a hub for manufacturers
talks.teaser: Explains how a procurement software company links engineering drawings to ERP systems for direct materials sourcing.
talks.summary:
The speaker's engineering finance work on Tesla's Model 3 showed how much procurement shaped financial performance, yet sourcing for about $30 billion of parts ran on spreadsheets, emails and a home-built ticketing process. Changes to one part's drawings could bring 500 to 2,000 emails between engineering, finance, procurement and suppliers. In one case a wire harness missing from a drawing led a supplier to seek a 25% cost increase, and a $2 per-car change on a door handle would add up to $20 million across 10 million Model 3s.

Lightsource, a software company the speaker co-founded, is presented as an AI procurement operating system for direct materials, meaning parts built into a product rather than office supplies. It sits between PLM and ERP systems, gathering drawings, bills of materials and supplier exchanges before pricing goes to the ERP for orders. Some customers run dozens of ERPs, so the company builds connectors across systems. Agent-style features include a sourcing co-pilot that helps set up events and evaluate quotes, while background tools extract terms from uploaded contracts.

The speaker argued that AI should augment buyers by automating tedious tasks, not replace them, since supplier relationships stay collaborative and human. He also described a spec to scale framework that runs from specification through sourcing to ongoing supply monitoring, including price and quality tracking after award.

talks.title: Debunking the SaaSpocalypse: What Is the Real Threat to SaaS Giants?
talks.teaser: Argues that AI-built tools are unlikely to topple big SaaS vendors, and that pricing models pose the real challenge.
talks.summary:
This podcast episode examines the idea of a "SaaSpocalypse," the fear that agentic AI and vibe coding tools will let frontline workers build their own applications and make large enterprise software vendors unnecessary. Don Flickinger, a TechTarget reporter who covers enterprise software, argues the fear is overstated. Major vendors are beating earnings projections even as their stocks fall, and he suggests the sell-off reflects investor nervousness rather than a genuine loss of demand.

He frames the question as a version of the long-running build-or-buy debate. Building in-house offers deep customization but requires paying engineers and maintaining the software indefinitely, while most companies prefer integrated suites. Quickly generated tools lack the security, governance, compliance and workflow depth that enterprises have built over decades, so large firms are unlikely to replace their platforms wholesale. Smaller organisations with simpler IT stacks may find self-built tools more practical.

The more pressing issue, he argues, is pricing. Seat licences are a core revenue source, yet AI agents generally do not need a seat, while consumption fees and pass-through charges from LLM providers can produce surprise bills. Salesforce is experimenting with agentic work units, a metric for measuring useful AI output, but it has not said how it will price them and is still defining what counts as work. Zendesk's tiered outcome-based pricing is cited as an earlier attempt. The takeaway is that customers will push back on opaque costs, so vendors offering clearer, more transparent pricing are likely to earn trust.

talks.title: IT Ops Query | AI, jobs and billionaires: Former Googler issues warnings
talks.teaser: A climate investor and former Google X executive links AI job shifts, economic design and political instability.
talks.summary:
In this episode of IT Ops Query, the guest, a climate investor who previously worked on product experience at Google X, discusses his book Climate Capital. He frames economics as a design problem and links three pressures: climate change, AI's threat to jobs, and political unrest. He argues that government regulation and labor unions have lost much of their power, leaving consumer demand as the main check on corporations, since coordinated boycotts can quickly hit quarterly results. For enterprise buyers without consumer input, he suggests becoming an activist shareholder.

The conversation then turns to household finances and AI in software work. He cites a rise in the share of US income going to housing from about 19% to 40% over 20 years, and says economic strain feeds political breakdown. On AI-generated code, he warns that shipping output without human review still creates security holes and technical debt, and that when the original developer has left, nobody can explain why a module works. He describes a "reverse centaur" setup, where people clean up after machines, and expects cheap swaps of mediocre roles for mediocre AI to cause visible failures.

Toward the end, he says claims that shareholders force harmful decisions should be tested by surveying them, and that current AI has not shown it can radically cut costs in heavy industry. He expects training energy for AI to fall by a factor of 10 every three to four years, mainly through software. His practical advice for enterprise leaders is to measure what customers and shareholders actually want, check AI output before release, and watch for dependence on foundation models that change without notice.

talks.title: Targeting AI: Navigating the generative AI landscape with two MIT profs
talks.teaser: Two MIT academics discuss generative AI's energy demands, workforce effects, and the gap between usefulness and profit.
talks.summary:
This podcast episode from AI Business features two MIT academics, Abel Sanchez and John Williams, who co-instruct an MIT Professional Education course and co-founded GenAI Global, a professional network for generative AI adoption. Sanchez explains that the network rests on the idea that learning works better with community. He contrasts MIT OpenCourseWare, where attrition is above 90%, with well-supported courses that reach over 90% completion. The guests also describe leaders struggling to set strategy because no playbook exists yet.

The middle of the conversation covers what Sanchez calls vibe living, where non-experts use natural language to work in fields they have not trained in, such as no-code hackathons. Williams turns to energy: hyperscalers are building power stations above 2 gigawatts, larger than a 1.7-gigawatt nuclear plant, and European electricity costs are roughly double the price he cites for Massachusetts. The guests then discuss layoffs, the value of keeping a human in the loop, and a reported finding that 95% of AI pilots fail, which they attribute to organisations rather than the technology.

The episode ends on the bubble question. The guests expect a wave that will continue, expect humans or other models to review the output of agentic systems, and separate whether the technology works from whether companies can make money from it. They agree to return for a fuller discussion of AI in education.

talks.title: Capgemini exec shares lessons from SAP agentic AI projects
talks.teaser: Describes how Capgemini deploys agentic AI on SAP systems, covering tools, integration, multi-agent work and adoption challenges.
talks.summary:
In this conversation with podcast host David Essex, Gian Luca Simeone, a Capgemini vice president and chief technology and innovation officer, explains how the firm applies agentic AI on SAP systems. He describes three focus areas for clients: speeding up SAP go-lives, lowering operational costs, and building people with the right skills and mindset. One project used SAP Juul Studio to build, in three weeks, agents that span SAP and non-SAP systems and automate procure-to-pay for an oil and gas company.

On tooling, he says Juul Studio is a low-code platform that business consultants can use alongside developers, with natural language instructions and optional code. For integration, Capgemini generally recommends staying on SAP's clean core model with BTP and Integration Suite, and building a library of business APIs so agents can replace older point-to-point data exchanges. Multi-agent orchestration remains experimental: agent-to-agent communication is not yet running in production, though a three-way project with SAP and Google is testing a new protocol. Other live cases include a Nordic utility's hyper-automation work and agents that help identify qualified vendors during request-for-quotation steps.

The biggest obstacles, he argues, are mindset, trust, security and data classification, so clean core principles and data quality are practical starting points. Looking ahead, he expects system integrators to automate much of project delivery and ERP systems to become semi-autonomous, with humans kept on the key decisions.

talks.title: Microsoft's Brendan Burns on the future of AI infrastructure
talks.teaser: Covers how AI is reducing developer toil, shaping Kubernetes, and moving cloud management toward intent-based infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with two areas where AI is changing how Microsoft's engineering teams work. The first is toil reduction: agents take on tasks developers find unappealing, such as major library upgrades that used to be deferred and left teams without security fixes. The second is easier summarization of large deployment data, with a chat interface in Azure that lets operators query resources in plain language. Chat is becoming a new interface alongside the portal, CLI and API, and custom MCP servers connect agents to an organization's own context.

On governance, suggestions must respect access control and Azure policy, including corporate naming rules, because enterprises still need control. Multicloud is treated as a long-standing demand, and Azure Arc is described as bringing AWS, GCP and on-premises resources into one view that AI can reason over. On Kubernetes, GPU management and group scheduling APIs are still maturing in beta, while open source projects such as Kaido let users serve models from a short declaration without becoming deployment experts. The speaker expects Kubernetes to become less visible over time, much as the Linux kernel now sits unseen beneath it.

Looking ahead, the key shift is rethinking what counts as hard. Small changes in legacy code that once skipped tests may now be expected to come with a generated test, and recurring changes can be written as prompts instead of documents sent to every team. For enterprise leaders, the advice is to use these tools personally so they learn where the value fits their own workflows.

talks.title: Enterprise Apps Unpacked: AI-human symbiosis could be key for enterprise AGI software
talks.teaser: Asks whether human-machine symbiosis, not replacement, is the route to general AI and what that means for enterprise software.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens by defining artificial general intelligence as AI that can match human understanding and apply knowledge to unfamiliar tasks, unlike today's narrow generative and agentic systems. The guest argues that generality means breadth across subjects while superintelligence means depth, and that progress is ongoing rather than a single milestone. He holds that current models capture only computational intelligence, omitting instinct, creativity and values, so humans must stay actively involved in shaping data and how systems are used.

He says his lab releases nothing until it can be shown mathematically to work and why. Humanics reverses the usual prompting pattern: the system asks people questions that draw out intuition and values, and contributors are paid for their data. He also describes RAIDS, a rogue AI detection system that flags when a model drifts from its intended behavior, likened to a smoke detector, and a venture that predicts which patients will miss medical appointments.

For enterprise software, he expects agents linked to email, health records and finances to make traditional interfaces and applications fade over the next few years. He acknowledges job displacement, offering micro-entrepreneurship and expert data work as partial answers, and warns that firms without agents will be left behind. The takeaway is that adoption will accelerate while effects on employees remain open questions.

talks.title: IT Ops Query: IBM Watsonx Orchestrate and the state of AI agent platforms
talks.teaser: Covers how Watsonx Orchestrate coordinates many AI agents and why integrations and governance slow production rollouts.
talks.summary:
An IBM vice president of product management discusses the Watsonx Orchestrate agent platform about nine months after its launch, a period in which most large IT vendors also released agent orchestration products. The conversation begins with how the platform differs from agent-building tools offered by other vendors. The guest argues that its focus is coordinating agents across many domains, clouds and on-premises systems, handling routing, tool selection, response validation and policy checks, and that it often works alongside rival platforms rather than replacing them.

The discussion then turns to what customers need next. Companies with dozens of agents need help choosing which one should take a request, and some processes, such as hiring steps with compliance requirements, must follow fixed sequences rather than open-ended agent decisions. Organisations also want governance over agents built in scattered teams, including evaluation thresholds that vary by use case and monitoring of latency and accuracy once agents are live. The guest says the usual obstacle to production is the back-end integrations rather than the agents themselves, particularly confirming that access control and context pass correctly to each connected system. Human approval steps, agent-assist summaries for staff in customer care, and agents listed in employee directories with named owners are also described.

The takeaway is that organisations should avoid committing to a single vendor, should require tracing and governance across agents wherever they run, and should prepare clean data and consistent access rules before expecting a quick move from pilot to production. The guest also suggests that routine manual work is shifting toward higher-value strategic tasks.

talks.title: IBM Watsonx Orchestrate and the state of AI agent platforms
talks.teaser: A product leader outlines multi-agent orchestration, governance tooling, and what slows enterprises moving AI agents to production.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens on a crowded market of agent orchestration offerings and positions IBM Watsonx Orchestrate around coordinating many agents across HR, sales, directory, and other backends rather than treating one vendor stack as the whole story. The guest describes routing employee requests to the right specialized agent, blending fully agentic flows with deterministic step sequences for regulated hiring, and scaling from a handful of collaborators to fifty or more agents that need intelligent handoffs.

Midway, emphasis shifts to operational reality: enterprises already harbor large agent portfolios built with disparate tools, and need visibility, evaluation thresholds that differ by risk (for example roughly ninety-eight percent versus ninety percent accuracy expectations), tracing, latency monitoring, and the ability to pull underperforming agents offline. Moving from quick pilots to production for tens of thousands of users is portrayed as months of integration work—API and MCP connectivity, consistent access control, clean data, and correct identity context when teams—not individuals—hold permissions.

The close covers deployment patterns (agents referenced in orchestrate while staying on their original runtime versus importing for deeper governance), guardrails when third-party agents participate, human-in-the-loop and agent-assist for customer care, emerging agent manager roles, and converting documented processes into starter agents through in-browser build tooling while keeping humans on higher-value strategic work.

talks.title: Future of data backup: Big data quality, long live TAPE, and out with 3-2-1
talks.teaser: Explains how AI is reshaping data backup, why tape still matters against ransomware, and how the 3-2-1 rule may need updating.
talks.summary:
The interview opens with the main data trends business leaders should watch heading into 2026. Aaron Sullivan, an editor who covers data technologies, says AI is changing backup work in two ways. It can automate scheduling, testing and anomaly monitoring, and it has raised the bar for data literacy, since staff now need to check what AI produces. Cloud repatriation is also pulling critical data, backups included, back on site for reasons of cost and security.

Turning to AI and backups, Sullivan explains that backup archives could be a source of clean, organised training data, but she has not yet seen concrete examples of companies doing this. Obstacles include backups that were neglected or not refreshed regularly, and the personal identifiable information they often contain, which makes privacy a concern. On big data, the emphasis has shifted from volume to quality: AI needs accurate, structured, error-corrected data with clear identifiers such as dates and IDs.

Sullivan argues that the question of whether tape is dead should be retired. Tape is offline, which protects against ransomware, and it offers large capacity at a reasonable price, so it still has business value. She also says the classic 3-2-1 rule, three copies on two media with one offsite, needs updating for modern threats, with variants that add an offline copy and zero-error verification. She would like to see an industry standard that makes backup easier for newcomers to understand.

talks.title: IT Ops Query: Kelsey Hightower's advice for platform engineers as AI looms
talks.teaser: Argues that platform engineering rests on skills and decisions, while AI mainly changes the surface layer.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with the state of platform engineering. The guest argues that the field has a shared vocabulary and common tools, but teams still struggle to use them well. Many organizations try to buy their way to new approaches without building the skills and discipline first, and most are building their first version of a system with no prior experience. He suggests that leaders make a clear decision on an approach, then invest in training and apprenticeship before setting deadlines.

On AI, he describes it as a surface technology that runs on the same hardware, operating systems, networks and vulnerabilities as before. He sees its practical value in translation: turning a plain-language question into a query, checking the result, and saving reusable shortcuts. For routine work he favors simple, deterministic programs. He gives examples such as a short Python script that removes logs older than 90 days, and he says an AI agent is unnecessary for a basic password reset. He also argues that earlier promises, such as serverless and no-ops, were overstated because no one has built a perfect system.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to find the inefficiencies in their own teams, such as difficulties with Kubernetes, networking or cost management, and to fix those with straightforward automation before reaching for AI. He encourages IT staff to ask what value they bring beyond machines and to refresh the fundamentals and tools they already have.

talks.title: Future of CIO strategy: The AI plateau, talent retention, and sustainability
talks.teaser: Covers how CIOs move AI from pilots to production, keep scarce senior talent, and build sustainability business cases.
talks.summary:
A host and Tim Murphy, a site editor covering IT strategy, discuss what chief information officers should prioritise heading into 2026. Murphy outlines three trends from his interviews: generative AI moving from experiments into production, retaining senior staff who know enterprise platforms deeply, and making a business case for sustainability rather than just reporting on it.

Murphy places many organisations in the trough of disillusionment on the Gartner hype cycle, where pilots stall because they use only part of the data, skip governance and fail to fit into workflows. On talent, he argues that senior people such as those who run Kubernetes clusters and those who manage governance models for AI agents are becoming more valuable. Pay alone will not keep them, so CIOs should clarify ownership during restructuring, be open about how AI will change roles, and invest in upskilling. He also notes that some organisations use AI to cut headcount, though many use it to raise productivity instead.

On sustainability, Murphy says leaders must show how green initiatives help the bottom line, given ESG skepticism in the US and EU rule rollbacks. AI can speed up sustainability reporting but consumes significant energy, so narrowing efforts to proven use cases helps. He closes by expecting agentic AI use cases to start showing business value next, roughly a step behind generative AI.

talks.teaser: Traces how a revenue AI platform shifted from predictive models to task-specific agents, and where agentic selling stands.
talks.summary:
Alon Rish, co-founder and chief product officer of Gong, describes how the company grew out of a sales problem at an earlier software firm. Deals were stalling even though the pipeline data looked healthy, and reading emails and listening to calls by hand did not scale, so the team set out to automate that analysis. Gong now presents itself as a revenue AI platform that brings forecasting, pipeline review, enablement and account planning into one place, and Rish says it serves about 5,000 customers.

The discussion covers how the technology has changed. Earlier, the company built its own models for each task. It now uses commercial large language models for generative work such as call briefs and conversational features, while keeping in-house models for jobs LLMs handle poorly, such as revenue prediction and speaker identification. Gong benchmarks each new feature before release and routes traffic among several LLM providers. Rish defines useful agents as narrow, well-defined tools embedded in existing workflows and kept under human supervision. He argues that fully autonomous selling is still far off, though parts of the job, such as product demos or training, could be automated.

Looking ahead, Rish says the aim is to roughly double frontline productivity over several years by removing administrative work. He also argues that a vendor's proprietary call and email data is a differentiator for specialized AI products, compared with general chat assistants. Planned work includes a training product, a companion for sellers, and research and content-generation agents.

talks.title: How AI amplifies resume fraud and other job seeker cheating
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning How AI amplifies resume fraud and other job seeker cheating.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this episode of Enterprise Apps Unpacked, host David Essex interviews analyst and consultant Brian Sommer (founder of TechVentive and former Accenture partner) regarding how artificial intelligence and related technologies amplify fraud and deception across the hiring lifecycle and workplace. Sommer outlines how readily accessible citizen AI tools, generative models, and automation enable job seekers, employees, contractors, and even nation-state actors to deceive employers faster, at greater volume, and in sophisticated new ways.

### Key Topics
- **Forms of Employment Deception**: Sommer defines fraud as an intent to deceive, categorizing manifestations such as resume misrepresentation (fabricating degrees or past roles), time theft (accepting pay without delivering required outputs), productivity/performance theater (pretending to work using tools like mouse jigglers), cheating on certification exams or employee training, and dual-employment schemes (holding multiple full-time roles simultaneously).
- **Citizen AI and ATS Inversion**: The widespread availability of low-cost generative AI enables mediocre or unqualified applicants to tailor resumes directly to job descriptions. Citing recent academic findings from major job board data, Sommer notes this dynamic causes employers to hire candidates in the top quintile 19% less often and candidates in the bottom quintile 14% more often, compressing differentiation and promoting previously undetected recruiting errors (PUREs).
- **High-End Threats and Nation-State Infiltration**: The discussion highlights nation-state actors, specifically North Korea, deploying deepfake visual overlays (projecting real-time altered visages with synchronized blinking and lip movements) and real-time speech translation during video interviews. These operations secure remote jobs to extract hard currency via local confederates and plant spyware or exfiltrate intellectual property.
- **Application Flooding and Process Breakdown**: Job seekers now deploy automated AI tools to submit thousands of applications (such as an example of a candidate applying to 5,000 jobs), spamming talent acquisition teams and breaking traditional filtering mechanisms.

### Technical Details & Countermeasures
- **Applicant Verification & Skills Testing**: Platforms like HireVue address untrusted self-reported resume data by performing digital, non-human, scalable skills assessments prior to moving candidates forward.
- **Cross-Referencing External Data**: Emerging detection methods analyze historical social media profiles (e.g., LinkedIn progression) and historical payroll bureau databases to flag discrepancies in job seniority, wage history, and employment gaps.
- **Cryptographic & Blockchain Credentials**: Earlier startup initiatives explored securing certified academic records on blockchain registries to permit instant validation.
- **Internal Auditing & A/B Testing**: Sommer advises employers to A/B test applicant tracking systems (ATS) against manual recruiter reviews using sample batches (e.g., 200 resumes) to evaluate filtering accuracy.

### Takeaways
Sommer argues that applying incremental AI tools on top of an already broken recruitment funnel will fail. Employers must adopt a 'trust but verify' posture, acknowledging that resumes represent unverified self-reported data. Organizations need to rethink the talent acquisition process fundamentally, monitor internal operational metrics to curb productivity theater and worker burnout, engage candidates in focus groups, and regularly evaluate emerging vendor countermeasures.

talks.title: AI data management and governance take center stage in 2026
talks.teaser: Looks ahead at AI data quality, governance and open-source interchange formats shaping enterprise tech plans in 2026.
talks.summary:
In this podcast interview, Rob Streche looks back at 2025 and ahead to 2026 with host Beth Pariso. He names the convergence around open table formats such as Iceberg and Delta, and the OSI schema interchange format Snowflake is promoting, as the most significant story. The earlier fight over who would own data catalogs has given way to a shared need to exchange data between platforms.

On security, he argues it has been an overlooked afterthought in the rush toward agents and agentic AI. He expects open governance from groups like the Linux Foundation, CNCF and Apache to bring rigor to projects such as MCP servers. He also points to infrastructure spending: GPU purchases need storage and networking behind them, cost optimization received little attention in 2025, and duplicate data and silos keep growing.

For 2026, he expects the quality, governance and security of data used by AI to be the central problems, and doubts that enterprises will push all their data into one vendor's repository. He sees agents changing how work gets done rather than simply replacing people, with reskilling and education lagging behind. He also highlights resilience and disaster recovery, pushed by regulation such as DORA. His practical message is to tie AI spending to measurable ROI and governance from the start.

talks.title: Targeting AI: Google AI exec says data is the next phase of generative AI
talks.teaser: Covers treating enterprise data as a product, tapping dark data, and grounding AI agents in trusted sources.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that generative AI has shifted attention from model size to the data those models depend on. The guest, a product manager for data and AI at Google Cloud, says many enterprises hold large amounts of unstructured material, such as documents, images and PDFs, that analytics teams never treated as analysis-ready. Generative tooling now makes that content usable, but it needs clear ownership, quality checks and governance.

Customer cases illustrate the change. A consumer goods company once spent months gathering global trend feeds; with a continuously refreshed data product, it spots emerging trends within minutes, and an agent can propose a marketing campaign. Telecom operator Optus moved from reviewing aggregated network reports by hand to autonomous analysis of granular data streams, which it uses to predict failures up to three weeks ahead and to open ServiceNow tickets with summaries for engineers. Instacart, with 17 million unique items, grounds its shopping agent in the product catalogue and each shopper's dietary needs through vector search.

Reliability comes from grounding, so models answer only from enterprise data retrieved through vector embeddings, with citations and lineage showing where figures originated. The speaker also argues AI should be brought into the data stack rather than sending sensitive records out, since staff pasting proprietary information into models is seen as a bigger risk than outside attackers. The takeaway is to treat data as a product and ground agents in trusted sources.

talks.title: Enterprise Apps Unpacked: How a distributor used AI-driven dynamic pricing for quick ROI
talks.teaser: Follows an electrical distributor's rollout of an AI pricing widget in its order entry screen, with results and lessons learned.
talks.summary:
An electrical and industrial distributor describes how its sales pricing had relied on fixed category and customer-segment rules plus salespeople's judgment, leading to inconsistent prices and slow reactions to swings in commodity costs such as copper and aluminum. After about two years of failed attempts with in-house data scientists and other partners, the company subscribed to Infor's data science team, which built a pricing widget into the order entry screen used by inside sales staff.

The widget shows a recommended margin with a minimum and maximum range, drawing on historical sales, competitor prices gathered from websites, commodity markets, inventory status and product category. The guest estimates the model is about 40 percent traditional analytics and 60 percent AI-driven learning, and says the aim is fairer, less arbitrary margins rather than across-the-board price increases. Early results cited include about $700,000 in new revenue, roughly $500,000 in margin improvement and a 1.3% gross margin increase.

The first version ran on the on-premises ERP and was built to move to the cloud version. A newer inventory model, live for about two weeks at recording, showed an early efficiency gain on the slowest-moving items, with fuller figures expected later. Challenges included experienced salespeople worried that the tool could harm long-standing customer relationships, and early product groupings from the vendor's data scientists that staff first pushed back on. Adoption spread as early adopters reported wins. In hindsight, the guest would have started with a bigger project.

talks.title: Deloitte experts: Internal controls key in ERP cloud migration
talks.teaser: Explains why internal controls matter when moving ERP finance systems to the cloud, and who owns them.
talks.summary:
This Enterprise Apps Unpacked podcast episode features Deloitte's Laura Bellinger, an audit and assurance partner, and David Reigns, who leads digital controls for ERP and cloud work. They discuss a point-of-view article arguing that companies moving finance systems to cloud ERP should design internal controls from the start, ideally during blueprinting, and have go-forward controls in place by go-live.

They explain that cloud adoption creates shared responsibility: the provider handles some controls while the customer keeps others, such as access security and change control, and should not assume a vendor has covered them. Controls can live in written policy, in configured software that enforces access rules, or in automation that flags unusual activity. Coverage spans financial accuracy, operational performance and regulatory compliance, with preventive, detective and corrective mechanisms. AI can scan large volumes of data for odd patterns and help with reconciliations and access reviews, but it still needs governance and clear accountability.

Responsibility is spread across three lines of defense, with executives such as the CFO and CIO setting expectations, business teams running daily controls, compliance and risk owning frameworks, and internal audit testing effectiveness. The conversation also notes that smaller firms can scale controls down while keeping the same principles, and that weak controls risk misstated financials, data breaches, compliance failures and reputational harm.

talks.title: Breaking News Analysis: Executive Order on AI in the Context of Global AI Race
talks.teaser: Breaks down a recent US executive order on AI, its clash with state laws, and its prospects for survival.
talks.summary:
The host and guest Michael Bennett, associate vice chancellor for data science and AI strategy, discuss a recent presidential executive order that sets out a national policy framework for artificial intelligence. The order lets the Commerce Secretary withhold funds from states that have AI laws and asks agencies such as the FCC and FTC to weigh actions that would override conflicting state rules. Bennett says states with such laws should not be surprised, since the administration has opposed state and local AI regulation for most of a year, and he expects them to resist. He also expects the fight to grow more intense as the midterm elections approach, with AI becoming a larger election issue.

On whether loosening oversight helps the United States win the AI race, Bennett says the outcome is hard to predict. He describes the approach as a traditionally American, minimal-regulation stance, contrasted with the European Union's far more aggressive rules and China's more restrictive model of control. He argues that US policy would be only one factor among many, given the global scale of capital, talent and government investment in AI development.

Asked whether the order would survive a change of administration, Bennett thinks it almost certainly would be overturned if a Democratic candidate wins. The takeaway is that federal and state conflict over AI rules is likely to stay a live, election-driven issue.

talks.title: 'Back to the Future' with self-hosted bare metal
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for 'Back to the Future' with self-hosted bare metal.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this episode of IT Ops Query, host Beth Pariso speaks with Rob Hirschfeld, CEO and co-founder of RackN, regarding the return to self-managed bare metal infrastructure and on-premises data centers. As enterprises grapple with unpredictable public cloud expenditures, VMware exit strategies following the Broadcom acquisition, and the immense demands of generative AI workloads, self-hosted hardware is re-emerging as a strategic priority. Hirschfeld outlines how contemporary bare metal operations diverge significantly from legacy 2005-era data centers, emphasizing modern automation, infrastructure-as-code, and robust operational processes.

### Key Topics
- **Cloud Repatriation and Cost Realities:** Enterprises with cloud-first strategies are finding cloud expenses harder to forecast and control. For stable workloads, purchasing, depreciating, and owning physical assets often provides superior economic value.
- **The Platform Engineering vs. Bare Metal Divide:** Modern platform engineering teams have largely developed an application-centric focus around Kubernetes and hosted cloud environments. Hirschfeld points out that these teams frequently lack the lower-level storage, networking, and hardware expertise needed to run physical infrastructure or execute a VMware exit.
- **The Challenge of VMware Exits:** Migrating away from VMware to alternatives like OpenShift virtualization requires extensive bare metal lifting. VMware offers decades of deep, standardized integration in advanced storage and networking that cloud-native orchestration frameworks do not fully replicate out of the box.
- **Modernizing Hardware Operations:** Self-managed infrastructure today does not mean reverting to manual scripts or USB drives. Practices such as rack-scale automation, API-driven out-of-band management (e.g., Dell iDRAC), GitOps, and repaving infrastructure are being applied directly to physical bare metal.
- **Generative AI Infrastructure Pressures:** Generative AI does not introduce a fundamentally different workload type, but it imposes extreme operational demands. High-cost systems ($250,000 to $500,000 per server) require complex configurations, smart NICs, RoCE/InfiniBand fabrics, and rigorous firmware management down to SSDs. Lengthy resets or misconfigurations can result in massive downtime and depreciation costs.
- **Data Sovereignty and Workload Co-mingling:** The cost of paying per token and the security risks associated with sending sensitive enterprise data to external third parties are pushing companies to bring AI inference on premises. In the long term, AI workloads and agentic systems are expected to co-mingle with standard business applications.

### Technical Details
- **Hardware Configuration and Out-of-Band Management:** Modern bare metal depends on API-driven out-of-band controllers like Dell's iDRAC. Hirschfeld notes real-world edge cases, such as vendors unexpectedly making boot sequence settings read-only in firmware updates, breaking automated provisioning.
- **AI Hardware Fabrics and Interconnects:** AI clusters demand tight integration of advanced NICs, RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet), and InfiniBand to facilitate shared memory across nodes, rendering off-the-shelf OEM profiles insufficient without continuous patching and automation.
- **Infrastructure as Code and Rack Repaving:** Utilizing declarative infrastructure-as-code patterns allows operators to tear down and rebuild entire racks programmatically, treating bare metal with cloud-native immutability.

### Takeaways
- **Focus on Day-Two Operations First:** Rather than hand-crafting pilots that fail to scale, organizations must establish clear operational processes for updating, patching, and automating bare metal early on.
- **Address the Skills Gap:** The industry faces a shortage of engineers experienced in physical infrastructure. Solving this requires standardizing operations and leveraging modular automation rather than relying on bespoke configurations or rigid converged vendor lock-in.
- **Maintain Infrastructure Autonomy:** Controlling physical infrastructure protects sensitive data sovereignty, mitigates uncontrollable cloud pricing, and preserves core organizational autonomy.

talks.title: Targeting AI: Securing autonomous enterprise agents in the age of generative AI
talks.teaser: Explains how securing autonomous AI agents differs from traditional enterprise security, and why visibility and governance matter.
talks.summary:
In this short interview recorded at an AI summit in New York, host Esther Shisu speaks with Arin Michaels, chief executive of an enterprise platform for AI agent governance and security. They begin with why securing agents differs from traditional security. Conventional programs focus on outsiders trying to break in, but agents also let authorized staff run tasks that an AI may mishandle through hallucination or unexpected behavior, producing bad outcomes. Protection therefore has to account for the agent itself, not only the human identity behind it.

The discussion covers the main threats to large businesses. Michaels points to damage to data and unintended consequences when agents run unchecked, along with prompt injection and similar exploits. He argues the conversation has shifted from generative AI worries about training data, which he considers largely solved, to agents that take actions rather than only make recommendations. Human oversight also comes up: teams can watch an agent closely at first, much as they would a new hire, and loosen review once its actions look sound. Visibility and governance over actions taken through MCP or other channels are presented as essential.

On regulation, he says enterprises face little rule-making about how they use their own internal data, while public-facing AI already draws regulatory attention. He expects companies to keep their agents secure because they have a strong interest in doing so. The practical takeaway is to treat agents as a distinct security concern, make their behavior observable, and reduce human review only as evidence of good conduct builds up.

talks.title: IT Ops Query: ServiceNow AI Maven on AI Agent Evolution
talks.teaser: A ServiceNow executive explains how enterprise AI agents handle IT service work and how governance fits in.
talks.summary:
The episode is an interview with Dorit Zilbershot, group vice president of AI experiences and innovation at ServiceNow, about the company's push into AI agents since its Xanadu platform launched in September 2024. She describes Apriel 2.0, a reasoning and multimodal model built with Nvidia that runs on one GPU, and argues that its visible reasoning lets customers audit answers and keep control over where compliance-sensitive data is processed.

On IT service management, she highlights two main use cases. The first is self-service, where agents reset passwords, order laptops or clear a browser cache on a user's desktop. The second is agent-assisted work, where built-in triage agents run initial log analysis before a human takes over. She also previews image and video input so an assistant can see what a user sees. Her description of the AI control tower, built on the CMDB, covers tracking AI models, agents, spending, ROI and security risk across an enterprise.

On why AI projects stall, she points to starting without a defined problem and to point tools that do not understand data or talk to each other. Her guidance is to use plain scripts or deterministic workflows when results must match every time, and agentic workflows only when the system must decide the next step, such as weighing priority and whether incidents repeat before escalating an SLA breach. She closes by noting that agent interoperability protocols are still in development and that she expects 2026 to bring broader adoption.

talks.title: IT Ops Query: Cloud-native platform engineering in the enterprise
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of IT Ops Query: Cloud-native platform engineering in the enterprise.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Recorded at KubeCon 2025 North America in Atlanta, this episode of IT Ops Query features host Beth Pariso interviewing Gaurav Saxena, Director of Engineering at a Fortune 20 automotive company. Saxena leads an infrastructure engineering team of 50 engineers focused on developer experience, productivity, an internal developer platform (IDP), data infrastructure, and site reliability engineering. The discussion centers on modernizing cloud-native core infrastructure, adopting CNCF projects to build developer platforms, implementing software supply chain security, and integrating AI workloads and agentic workflows into platform engineering.

### Key Topics
- **Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs):** Establishing declarative interfaces and operational guardrails so developers can provision infrastructure without needing to navigate underlying Kubernetes details.
- **Software Supply Chain Security:** Utilizing cryptographic signing, provenance tracking, and policy enforcement across CI/CD pipelines using tools like Sigstore, Cosign, and Kyverno.
- **AI Infrastructure & Model Routing:** Supporting enterprise AI workloads with GPUs, private LLMs, and intelligent context-aware traffic management tools such as Envoy AI Gateway.
- **Agentic AI in Operations:** Employing multimodal AI agents and MCP servers to assist developers with platform onboarding, triaging production incidents, and vulnerability scanning alongside humans in the loop.

### Technical Details
- **Platform Abstraction & Management:** The platform leverages CNCF graduated and incubating projects including Crossplane, OpenTelemetry, and KubeVela. Crossplane provides a Kubernetes-driven control plane to manage hyperscaler cloud resources. Combined with KubeVela specifications, developers define declarative requirements (e.g., databases, load balancers, messaging) while the platform team handles access control lists, availability zones, and underlying Kubernetes objects.
- **Supply Chain Security & Admission Control:** Following the OpenSSF baseline, the organization adopts Sigstore and Cosign within CI/CD pipelines to generate cryptographically signed Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs), verify provenance, and record metadata on public ledgers. To address vulnerabilities discovered after build artifacts sit in registries, Kyverno functions as policy-as-code integrated with Kubernetes admission controllers to reject non-compliant images.
- **AI Workload Routing and Serving:** To prevent enterprise data leakage, the organization relies on open-source, private LLMs with strict guardrails. Saxena highlights the recently released Envoy AI Gateway—acting as an intelligent Layer 7 proxy capable of context-aware routing, rate limiting, and optimizing inference cost and latency across models—alongside solo.io's agent workflow tooling, Knative, and KServe (which reached incubating status).

### Takeaways
Security, data sovereignty, and observability must be treated as first-class citizens rather than afterthoughts when architecting enterprise platforms. Integrating agentic workflows can significantly reduce developer cognitive load and expedite mean-time-to-resolution (MTTR) during outages, provided organizations maintain a human-in-the-loop approach and balance developer freedom with rigorous governance.

talks.title: Targeting AI: AI's Role in B2B Commerce on Alibaba.com
talks.teaser: A general manager outlines how AI supports complex B2B sourcing, supplier matching and buyer trust on Alibaba.com.
talks.summary:
In this podcast interview, Justin Lou, who runs Alibaba.com's operations in the US, explains how artificial intelligence is being applied to business-to-business sourcing. He argues that B2B buying is far more involved than consumer shopping, because buyers weigh many factors such as lead times, tiered pricing, shipping terms and compliance certificates before choosing a supplier.

He outlined three main areas where AI helps. The first is interpreting complex buyer requests and matching them to the right suppliers, drawing on a supplier database built over 26 years. The second is automating follow-up conversations with factories through chatbots and comparison tables. The third is internal work, such as live translation in multi-time-zone meetings and analysis of sales conversations. He also described Axio, a separate AI sourcing platform launched in 2025 for product research and supplier outreach, which he said has over 2 million users.

Asked about trust, he said the platform relies on trade assurance to protect payments and handle disputes and quality issues, and that AI is used to spot inaccurate listings across roughly 200 million products. He concluded that AI matters most for complex, customized or heavily regulated purchases, while standardized goods change less. The takeaway is that data accuracy and payment protection are central to AI in high-value cross-border commerce.

talks.title: Google union organizer on AI job impact, working conditions
talks.teaser: Explores how AI reshapes jobs and pay, from data-labeling contractors to automated suspensions and union campaigns.
talks.summary:
Shannon Wait, a senior organizer with the Alphabet Workers Union, joins David Essex on Enterprise Apps Unpacked to discuss a wave of layoffs that companies have tied to AI. She argues that the innovation story around AI hides job losses, and she points to software vendors that linked cuts directly to automation. Her own history starts in 2021, when she worked for a contractor at a Google data center in South Carolina and found that her pay and advancement lagged far behind Google's own staff. After she began organizing, she was suspended with pay, then won an unfair labor practice case and returned to her job.

The conversation then turns to the people who test and rate AI products, known as raiders, who work for contractors on Google, Meta, Amazon and other platforms. Organizing them led Google's supplier to raise their pay to $15 an hour by February 2024, without a union contract. Her survey of more than 150 workers found that 52% believe they are building products that replace other jobs, and 36% believe they are helping replace their own. She also described automated performance suspensions, unpaid downtime, and how staffing agency fees and lobbying make worker protections harder to win.

Looking ahead, she backed California's No Robo Bosses Act, which the governor recently vetoed, and a federal bill requiring quarterly reporting of AI-related job losses. She praised a neutrality agreement between the AFL-CIO and Microsoft and urged workers in finance and other sectors to organize, and states to attach labor standards to new data center projects.

talks.title: Oracle's Sudha Raghavan on AI's infrastructure renaissance
talks.teaser: Explains how AI demand is reshaping data center power, networking and GPU cluster scale at Oracle.
talks.summary:
Sudha Raghavan, a senior vice president at Oracle who runs its AI infrastructure platform, describes how AI is changing enterprise infrastructure buying. Unlike earlier cloud purchases of commodity hardware on subscription terms, companies make large upfront investments and plan years ahead. Demand for GPU capacity is outpacing supply, with four of the top five large training models said to run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and inference demand now growing alongside training.

The conversation then turns to power, water and networking. Raghavan says Oracle uses closed-loop, non-evaporative cooling and is building more liquid-cooled GPU racks. She also describes storing energy on site so that the large swings in load caused by AI workloads do not fall entirely on the grid. On networking, she outlines Acceleron, which uses RDMA over converged Ethernet and converged network interface cards, and ZPR, which lets teams define network security as policies that AI engineers can manage without separate firewall coordination. Multiplanar networking lets a workload keep running at reduced bandwidth when part of the fabric fails, instead of restarting from a checkpoint.

On scale, she discusses Zettascale 10, which she describes as 800,000 GPUs in one cluster across a 1.5 GW data center, with latency guarantees under 10 microseconds, and an AMD 50,000 GPU supercluster. Her takeaway is that building at this scale pushes suppliers, builders and power providers toward templated designs, and that more chip providers and regions will be needed as demand keeps outrunning supply.

talks.title: Enterprise Apps Unpacked: AI could save manufacturing from the baby boomer exodus
talks.teaser: Explores how AI co-pilots can preserve veteran factory know-how and attract younger workers to manufacturing jobs.
talks.summary:
The Enterprise Apps Unpacked podcast explores how AI could help manufacturers facing labor shortages as experienced workers retire and fewer young people consider factory jobs. The host asks whether AI automation will simply cut jobs, and the guest, Alex Sandival, CEO of Alli, argues that AI co-pilots can instead preserve the know-how of veteran workers and keep production lines running.

He explains that workflows captured in systems from spreadsheets to enterprise applications, along with tribal knowledge shared in chats and recorded conversations with worker consent, can feed a knowledge graph that suggests the next step. Alli's platform sits between ERP and manufacturing execution systems, combining production orders with machine and process signals to train models for goals such as fewer rejections or better yield. In process manufacturing, where one line may have over 10,000 parameters, he says workers can oversee more lines while humans still review and approve AI decisions.

For practitioners, he recommends deciding whether to build or buy, then starting with one costly problem such as a high rejection rate, instrumenting the relevant data, and working with partners where needed. He also describes closed-loop automation, where models adjust machines after human approval, and expects people to review the work of AI agents. He argues that presenting factory work as data-driven, tech-enabled and visibly impactful could draw younger workers back.

talks.title: AI could save manufacturing from the baby boomer exodus
talks.teaser: Explains how an AI co-pilot could capture retiring factory workers' know-how and help attract new workers to manufacturing.
talks.summary:
The host opens with the worry that AI will cost jobs, then looks at a more hopeful case in manufacturing, where retiring baby boomers, reluctant young graduates and reshoring have left plants short of skilled staff. His guest, Alex Sandival, argues AI can hold on to the tacit know-how of experienced workers, the kind of sense a plant manager gets from listening to a machine. He says this knowledge can be gathered from workflow records, spreadsheets and enterprise systems, plus conversations, with workers' consent.

He describes a platform layered over ERP and execution systems that combines production orders with machine signals such as temperature, pressure and vibration. A co-pilot then recommends or adjusts the next step. In food and beverage, where a single line can have over 10,000 parameters, models need process rules, such as how one variable affects another, to make sound decisions. He advises companies to decide whether to build or buy, since homegrown projects often fail, and to start with one costly problem, such as a high rejection rate. He sees closed-loop automation as the next step, with humans approving changes from outside the loop.

Sandival expects repetitive manual factory roles to disappear while new work emerges in capturing machine data, structuring knowledge and training predictive models. Training platforms and AR or VR can teach workers hands-on tasks in 3D. He argues manufacturers must reframe factory careers as data-driven, tech-enabled work with visible real-world impact to attract younger workers, and must build data foundations now.

talks.title: IT Ops Query: How GitHub Code Quality connects to AppSec
talks.teaser: Explains how GitHub's new code quality checks tie into application security, and how AppSec and development teams are converging.
talks.summary:
Host Beth Pariso and analyst Katie Norton discuss GitHub's public preview of code quality checks, which use its static analysis engine to flag maintainability and reliability problems in several languages. Norton argues that security is one dimension of overall application quality, and that QA, AppSec and development teams increasingly coordinate on both. She sees value in running these checks inside the coding agent alongside autofix, since code quality tools have historically been noisy and early fixes keep issues out of the testing backlog.

The discussion then turns to the market. Norton points to vendors moving into adjacent territory, including a newer code quality product from another security company and Sonar's move from code quality into application security. She says GitHub leans on partners for gaps such as dynamic testing and supply chain security, and that its platform ambitions force trade-offs between building natively and partnering. Norton describes application security as long siloed, which has driven interest in tools that bridge developers, QA and security operations.

On AI governance, Norton says most organizations are still early, with security, privacy and governance as their top concerns. Her main advice is to start with visibility, much as API discovery came first, and only then add policy and controls. She sees GitHub as well placed to offer that visibility and governance for software development, while noting that AI tools still need external checks even when AI is used to secure AI.

talks.title: How GitHub Code Quality connects to AppSec
talks.teaser: Discusses how code quality checks overlap with application security and how AI agents shift enterprise governance.
talks.summary:
This episode, recorded on location at GitHub Universe, looks at GitHub's public preview of code quality checks. The feature uses its static analysis engine to flag maintainability and reliability problems in Java, C, Python, JavaScript, Go and Ruby. The guest, Katie Norton, argues that security is one dimension of overall application quality, and that QA, AppSec and developer teams increasingly coordinate on it. She points to other vendors moving the same way, including a security company that launched a code quality product and Sonar, which expanded from code quality into application security.

The discussion then turns to why the feature matters in practice. Code quality tools have historically been noisy, so the appeal of GitHub's approach is running the checks through its coding agent inside the developer workflow, paired with autofix, so issues can be fixed before they reach a testing backlog. The conversation also covers how application security has been too siloed, the push toward platforms such as ASPM, and the partnerships GitHub uses to fill gaps like DAST and software supply chain security.

Later, the conversation moves to AI governance. Most organizations are still early in moving AI experiments into production, and security, privacy and governance are their top concerns. The guest's advice is to reuse lessons from earlier technologies, starting with visibility into which models, assistants and shadow tools are in use, then adding policy and controls. The takeaway for practitioners is that AI-generated code still needs external checks rather than trust in the platform alone.

talks.title: Breaking News Analysis: Nvidia's $5 trillion valuation reflects the AI market
talks.teaser: Analyzes Nvidia's $5 trillion valuation as a sign of AI market growth, weighing bubble risk, job impacts and monopoly concerns.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with news that Nvidia has reached a market valuation of $5 trillion, becoming the first company to do so. Ray Wong, of Constellation Research, argues that the figure reflects where the AI market currently stands. He points to data center buildouts, large compute commitments and sovereign AI deals as reasons he expects the valuation to keep rising over the next few years, and he compares Nvidia's value with the combined market caps of the top tech stocks and the US economy.

On whether an AI bubble exists, Wong says the market is in the middle of a boom. He would call it a bubble only once no one can pay for the AI being built, and he does not think that point has arrived. He is concerned that employment in other industries is flat or falling as AI spreads, with few new AI jobs appearing yet. He suggests trades, robot servicing and new kinds of human-machine work could emerge. He also describes small AI-native companies with very few staff reaching large recurring revenue, which he says both cannibalize and disrupt existing businesses.

Asked whether Nvidia could face monopoly accusations, Wong says some of its deal structures, chip allocation practices and circular investments could be alleged to be monopolistic. He expects such claims to be held back while the US and China compete over AI, and he sees that rivalry as a key reason the company is being supported.

talks.teaser: Explores how IoT, digital twins and AI are used to cut energy use, and what slows sustainability projects down.
talks.summary:
Peter Veaser, chief digital officer of Schneider Electric, explains that sustainability depends on a set of technologies working together rather than one product. He describes IoT sensors feeding a data platform that hosts a digital twin of the electrical system, with analytics layered on top and AI taking a growing share. Earlier IoT efforts were built as siloed stacks, and the company has since moved them onto a common platform that its Resource Advisor product uses.

As generation shifts from big plants to millions of rooftop solar sources, batteries and electric vehicles, the grid needs metering, forecasting and AI-driven control to stay stable. Two examples were offered: a new German headquarters designed to be CO2 neutral, and a Shanghai factory recognised as a World Economic Forum lighthouse, where time to market for customer orders was shortened by 63% and defects needing rework fell by about 80%. For data centres, the company pointed to liquid cooling from an acquired specialist, predictive maintenance and AI-driven energy optimisation.

He argued that technology is rarely the main obstacle. The harder problems are choosing high-value use cases, linking fragmented data so AI can scale, and changing business processes and people's habits. Schneider's approach starts from the outcome and its KPIs, then picks fit-for-purpose technology, including frugal AI aimed at net energy savings. He closed cautiously optimistic, noting that existing technologies could cut emissions by up to 70% and save 10 to 15 gigatons of CO2 a year if applied well.

talks.summary:
This episode of TechTarget's Targeting AI podcast features a Salesforce executive who leads Agentforce product management and the founder of a healthcare provider that uses the platform. They start by defining what being AI first means for each organization. The provider's leader says it applies AI wherever it can so clinicians have more time with patients. He points to a diabetes pilot in which 49 of 50 patients had diabetes reversed within 12 weeks.

The middle of the conversation covers why the practice chose agents over older predictive tools or simple chatbots, combining automation, predictive models and generative AI. Examples include an agent where providers rehearse empathetic planning conversations and receive feedback, scheduling tools that route patients to clinicians, and a meal-planning flow that builds recipes and shopping lists in minutes. The Salesforce side reports more than a million and a half agentic conversations on its own help site, and about 70% of administrative tasks in a performance cycle handed to agents.

Trust, data connection and agent management are presented as the sequence customers move through, and the provider noted early deployment friction that Salesforce fixed after feedback. Both sides stress tying agents to a clear KPI and measuring hard revenue or expense changes. The episode ends with the suggestion that AI-supported peer counselors could widen mental health care.

talks.teaser: Explores how enterprise customers adopt Rovo AI agents, search and chat, and what early workflow gains look like.
talks.summary:
In this IT Ops Query podcast interview, Atlassian's head of AI product reviews how its Rovo AI has developed in the six months since the spring Team conference. He explains that Rovo was folded into the platform for nearly every paying subscriber, a shift he sees as a key driver of adoption. He reports over three million monthly users across the product line, with Rovo search usage up over a hundred times and chat up 50 times.

Turning to engineering, he ties the DX acquisition to visibility across the development cycle, noting that developers spend only part of their day writing code, and says the aim is to find slow steps that AI can ease. For Rovo Dev, now generally available, he describes proactive pull request recommendations built from backlog issues, with customers charged a credit only when a suggestion is accepted. Early governance features include evaluations, usage insight and controls that limit an agent's visibility to chosen groups.

On remaining barriers, he points to getting tools into users' hands under each company's standards, which led to an Atlassian-hosted language model and role-based access. He also raises the need for norms that treat agents as accountable teammates. He closes with a customer example in which an IT team built an agent that checks equipment cabinet photos against documented standards and drafts remediation priorities, which he presents as a sign that audits could change.

talks.title: Atlassian Rovo AI grows to 3 million monthly users
talks.teaser: Atlassian's Rovo AI leader shares usage growth, agent adoption hurdles and advice for enterprise teams.
talks.summary:
In this interview, Jamil Valani, vice president and head of AI product at Atlassian, reviews the company's progress on its Rovo AI offerings over the six months since Atlassian began giving Rovo to all paying subscribers. He reports more than 3 million monthly users across the product line, Rovo search usage up more than 100 times, Rovo chat usage up 50 times, and search relevance improved by over 20 percent.

He points to agent activity as the clearest sign of value: over 800,000 business workflows accelerated through agents last month, a 50% month-over-month increase, and about 9,000 agents created in that month. Studio now lets creators build agents, automations and Forge apps from natural language. He also discusses DX, the engineering intelligence company Atlassian acquired, which is meant to give visibility into development cycles, and Rovo Dev's general availability with a chargeback model tied to successful, accepted pull request recommendations. One customer example is Tempo, whose IT team built an agent that analyzes equipment cabinet photos against Confluence standards.

Valani names two obstacles to enterprise agent adoption: getting tools to end users with role-based controls and, for regulated customers, a hosted LLM option, plus the new etiquette of treating agents as accountable teammates. His advice is to find one painful, recurring task, pilot an agent on it, and share what works, with leadership modeling the use.

talks.title: Enterprise Apps Unpacked: Why AI Search is the New Corporate Learning Powerhouse
talks.teaser: Argues that AI-powered search is reshaping corporate learning and could make traditional learning management systems obsolete.
talks.summary:
In this Enterprise Apps Unpacked podcast episode, host David Essex talks with Josh Buren about a shift he sees in workplace learning: employees asking AI-powered search tools questions as they work, instead of moving through fixed courses. Buren contrasts the traditional classroom-style model of corporate training, which is slow, hard to personalize, costly to build and difficult to translate, with a user enablement model in which content is loaded into an AI platform that answers questions and points back to its source material.

Buren describes early evidence from about 20 clients, including an insurer and an airline building a new academy. Some load their existing course libraries into these systems, while others add recorded interviews with experts directly, keeping compliance courses in the legacy learning management system. He also cites usage of his own AI assistant, Galileo, by roughly six or 7,000 people at about 500 companies, with questions ranging from recruiting and skills taxonomies to coaching underperforming staff. He argues that consumer chatbots are unsuitable for company data, so AI vendors are licensing their technology for internal use, and that learning tools and knowledge management systems are likely to converge.

For practitioners, Buren advises learning and development teams to test these tools hands-on, expect legacy learning platforms to be retired gradually, and offer content in multiple formats. He suggests that routine content production will shrink while people move toward higher-level design and management, and that workers will need to learn how to coach and check AI output.

talks.title: Targeting AI Breaking News: CoreWeave Lands $14.2 Billion Deal with Meta
talks.teaser: Unpacks the CoreWeave and Meta GPU compute deal, the economics of AI inference, and what it means for enterprises.
talks.summary:
In the first episode of the Targeting AI news podcast, host and guest Torson Vogue of Omdia discuss a CoreWeave deal with Meta, reported as $14.2 billion, that broke that morning. Although Meta runs large data centers, CoreWeave can supply GPUs at peak times, keep them well utilized, and secure the power and cooling involved, so Meta can focus on building AI rather than becoming a GPU provider.

The discussion then turns to cost. The guest compares the arrangement with an OpenAI compute deal with Oracle spanning five years, while the CoreWeave contract runs over six. The guest notes that AI labs are largely venture funded and often must subsidize inference to keep usage growing, and encourages developers to use heavy inference to improve their applications. They also point to the market impact: CoreWeave's stock jumped that day, and demand for power, GPUs, talent and data center space is outrunning supply. Specialized providers gain an edge through scale, low-latency networking and custom Kubernetes scheduling plugins, which are hard for rivals to replicate.

In closing, they return to Meta. The guest suggests that buying capacity from several vendors is a way to hedge bets and bring in outside expertise. At this scale, any company running such infrastructure effectively becomes an enterprise vendor, and each organization must decide which parts to handle in-house and where to rely on outside help. The episode ends with a brief sign-off.

talks.title: 5 Uses for AI in Disaster Recovery
talks.teaser: Explains five ways AI can support disaster preparation, response and recovery, from early warning to crisis communication.
talks.summary:
Disaster recovery teams rarely see a disaster coming, and this short video argues that AI can help at several points in the recovery lifecycle. The first use is prediction: models sift historical and live data, such as weather patterns, server load and other anomalies, to flag signs of disruption earlier, which gives IT staff more time to warn the business and cut the chance of downtime. The second is security, where AI-driven tools watch network traffic, learn about new threats, and block suspicious activity before it spreads.

When an incident hits, the video describes automated recovery, where systems detect anomalies and trigger predefined actions such as copying critical data to another location, rerouting traffic or activating failover. It also covers resource planning: by mapping dependencies, AI can suggest the most efficient recovery path and the order in which systems should come back online to limit cost and disruption. The fifth use is crisis communication, with automated alerts to staff, live status updates on social media and chatbots that answer questions when human support is unavailable.

The video is cautious. It advises against using a general chatbot to write a disaster recovery plan for now, and its closing point is that AI should amplify human responders rather than replace them. Viewers come away with a list of concrete places to test AI in recovery workflows, with people still making the final calls.

talks.title: What CISOs Need to Know About Shadow AI
talks.teaser: Explains the risks of unapproved generative AI use and outlines governance, monitoring and training steps for CISOs.
talks.summary:
The video opens by explaining that generative AI tools are easy for anyone to use, which creates risk when staff adopt unapproved ones, a problem known as shadow AI. The narrator lists its consequences as data exposure, compliance gaps and weaker quality in business offerings, and places responsibility for AI governance with the CISO.

The middle presents a survey by CySafe and the National Security Alliance, in which over 38% of employees reported sharing sensitive information with AI tools and 52% said they had received no training on safe use. Suggested responses include monitoring tools that find and can block unsanctioned AI, an audit strategy tracking how, when and by whom AI is used, and a governance framework that states which tools are permitted. Guardrails should be clear without being overly restrictive; a healthcare provider might allow AI for scheduling but not patient data processing or clinical decisions. Defining AI risks within existing frameworks makes accountability easier to trace.

The closing point is education. Staff need ongoing training, workshops and cross-team collaboration, and open communication helps departments learn compliance expectations from one another. The video concludes that eliminating shadow AI is unrealistic, but these measures help CISOs address threats and give organizations a foundation for managing AI as it changes.

talks.title: Targeting AI: Why Capital One Prefers Open Source | The Importance of Data for Banking
talks.teaser: Covers how Capital One builds enterprise AI on open-weight models customized with its own data, and guardrails for agents.
talks.summary:
Prem Natharajan, chief scientist and head of enterprise AI at Capital One, explains how the bank approaches AI as a platform-centric effort in a regulated industry. He describes starting with internal tools, including a generative AI agent assist platform used by more than 20,000 customer support agents, where first-answer relevance rose from 84% to 93%. The bank later launched an agentic chat assistant for automotive loan customers, which dealers use to answer questions and book test drives at any hour.

For safety, he says agentic systems build on decades of model risk management and add runtime guardrails, observability and human oversight, with open-source guardrail tools helping. Capital One favors open-weight language models and customizes them with proprietary data through prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning, which he says let several high-impact use cases reach production. He credits the bank's early focus on data and its move to a single public cloud for making this possible.

On return on investment, he argues that inference costs fell more than a thousandfold over about 22 months at equal benchmark performance, so tracking associate feedback matters more than early calculations. He presents regulation as a guideline that makes deployments more durable, pointing to an agent tool rolled out over 17 to 18 months with a pause to fix issues. The takeaway is to scale carefully and learn as you go.
