talks.title: Impact of COVID-19 on Storage Spending
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh how COVID-19 reshaped storage budgets, cloud and as-a-service buying, flash demand and NVMe adoption.
talks.summary:
A panel moderated by TechTarget publisher Jillian Coffin examines how the COVID-19 pandemic changed enterprise storage spending. The discussion starts from a global IT priority study fielded in December 2019 and January 2020, which showed almost 40% of respondents ranking cloud storage as their top area of investment and storage as a service climbing into the top five. Panelists Marc Staimer, Camberley Bates and Ken Steinhardt describe buyers who want flexibility, agility and cost control rather than long lock-in deals.

The conversation then turns to the pandemic itself. A follow-up survey found 52% of budgets flat and 10% of respondents increasing spend, with remote work enablement, cloud and security easiest to justify, while hiring and on-premises refreshes were harder to get approved. Flash research activity fell almost 60% from the fourth quarter into the second quarter before recovering. Panelists also discussed pay-as-you-grow consumption models that reduced the need for on-site service visits, and expected NVMe over Fabrics to converge with core NVMe in version 2.0 of the specification.

The panel closes with modernization themes: cost reduction and consolidation, containers, which one panelist put at under 15% adoption but expected to grow, multi-cloud and hybrid support, and separating data management from the storage hardware. The practical takeaway is that vendor choice increasingly depends on time to value and purchasing flexibility as much as on the underlying media.

talks.title: Wi-Fi 6 vs. Wi-Fi 5: Comparing Wireless Standards
talks.teaser: Compares Wi-Fi 6 with Wi-Fi 5 across access point capacity, spatial streams, frequency bands, data rates and multi-user MIMO.
talks.summary:
The video asks whether Wi-Fi 6 lives up to its hype by setting it against Wi-Fi 5, the wireless standard that has been dominant since 2014. It notes that many organizations still run networks built on Wi-Fi 5 while Wi-Fi 6 gains ground after its 2018 release and quick product launches. The presenter frames the comparison around five areas where the newer standard changes things.

The first area is access point capacity. Wi-Fi 6 adds OFDMA, a variant of the OFDM scheme used in Wi-Fi 5, which lets an access point serve several clients at once instead of one client per channel, improving efficiency and response times. Next comes spatial streams: Wi-Fi 5 tops out at four, while Wi-Fi 6 supports up to eight. On frequency bands, Wi-Fi 5 relies on 5 GHz, whereas Wi-Fi 6 uses both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, which the video links to better throughput.

The video then compares peak data rates, with a goal rate of about 6.9 Gbps for Wi-Fi 5 and 9.6 Gbps for Wi-Fi 6. Finally, it covers multi-user MIMO. Both generations use it, but Wi-Fi 5 is downlink-only while Wi-Fi 6 is bidirectional, supporting simultaneous uploads and downloads. The closing segment argues that Wi-Fi 6 will matter for keeping connectivity fast and secure as Internet of Things devices spread, and invites viewers to weigh in on its path to mainstream adoption.

talks.title: NOR vs. NAND Flash Memory
talks.teaser: Compares NOR and NAND flash memory, covering cell wiring, read and write speed, power draw and typical device uses.
talks.summary:
The video asks whether fast reads or fast writes matter more, and answers that it depends on the type of flash memory. It introduces NOR and NAND as two kinds of non-volatile memory and explains how their cells are wired differently. In NOR, each cell has one end tied to a source line and the other to a bit line, which resembles a NOR gate. In NAND, several cells are chained in a series arrangement, similar to a NAND gate.

That wiring drives the trade-offs. NOR can reach every byte in its range, so it reads randomly and quickly, but its larger cells make erasing and writing slower and raise its cost. NAND cells are smaller, cheaper and offer higher capacity. It erases and writes faster but reads more slowly, and it is more efficient for writes, erases and sequential reads. On power, NOR needs more energy to turn on but draws much less standby power once running.

In practice, NOR suits low-capacity, high-reliability roles such as scientific instruments and medical devices, while NAND fits high-capacity uses like digital cameras, USB drives and SD cards. Many smartphones and tablets combine both, using NOR to boot the operating system and a removable NAND card for other storage. The video closes by noting that NAND comes in five major types and invites viewers to share other use cases.

talks.title: Managed vs. Unmanaged Switches: What's the Difference?
talks.teaser: Compares managed and unmanaged network switches on control, security, features, and cost for different organizations.
talks.summary:
A network switch connects devices such as computers, printers and wireless access points so they can exchange data packets. This short video contrasts managed switches, where each port can be set and the network can be configured, monitored and controlled, with unmanaged switches, which auto-negotiate port parameters and require no setup. Managed models typically add Spanning Tree Protocol support, VLANs, bandwidth rate limiting, port mirroring and quality of service, but they demand administrators who understand network configuration and monitoring.

Unmanaged switches keep a fixed configuration yet still maintain a MAC address table, which reduces broadcast traffic and the collisions it can cause. Their security is minimal, mainly lockable port covers that guard against physical tampering. Managed switches offer stronger protections, including network monitoring and control, 802.1x authentication, port security and private VLANs.

Cost is the other major difference. Unmanaged switches are inexpensive, roughly fifty to a hundred dollars depending on port count, but few are suitable for enterprise use. Managed switches range from about $150 to $2,800 per port. The video concludes that unmanaged switches generally suffice for home offices and small businesses, while managed switches fit larger enterprise networks.

talks.title: Quantum Computing: 4 Things You Need to Know
talks.teaser: Explains four key points about quantum computing, from its threat to current encryption to its practical uses and limits.
talks.summary:
The video contrasts classical computers, which store information as zeros or ones, with quantum computers that use qubits able to represent both states at once. It cites Google's 2019 claim that its quantum machine solved a problem in a time that would take the world's fastest supercomputer an extremely long time, and notes that large technology firms are investing heavily in the field.

The presenter then covers four points. First, quantum machines could threaten the public-key math that protects sensitive government and corporate data, since calculations that would take classical computers an enormous span of time might run in minutes; IBM is working on quantum-safe algorithms in response. Second, the speed suits problems involving huge datasets and atomic-scale chemistry, such as drug manufacturing and molecular research, though experts expect few practical applications for at least a decade. Third, quantum systems are not meant to replace ordinary computers, which remain better for tasks like email and desktop publishing. Fourth, simulation work in pharmaceuticals, finance and other industries may bring early business value.

The talk closes by noting the hardware barrier: these machines need extreme cold near absolute zero, which makes owning one impractical for most organisations. Cloud access offered by IBM, AWS and others lets businesses and researchers prepare for a quantum future now, and viewers are invited to consider how it might affect their own organisations.

talks.title: What is Data Protection?
talks.teaser: Explains how snapshots, replication and cloud services protect data against media, storage and data center failures.
talks.summary:
Data protection means safeguarding critical information so that a business loses as little as possible, with the aim of keeping data intact and available. A strategy usually blends backup, disaster recovery and business continuity techniques, alongside areas such as cybersecurity management, ransomware prevention and regulatory compliance. The main goals are shielding data from compromise and restoring it after corruption.

The talk walks through four failure scenarios. For media failure, synchronous mirroring, freeze protection, erasure coding or replication keep data reachable when a storage device dies. For corruption or accidental deletion, point-in-time snapshots let a clean copy be mounted and restored almost instantly, and modern storage can keep hundreds of them without a significant performance hit. For a storage system failure, replicating snapshots to secondary systems, sending only the blocks that changed, keeps a standby ready if the primary fails.

The final scenario is the loss of an entire data center, which calls for a full disaster recovery plan. Snapshot replication can work here but may be expensive, so cloud replication and backup services are presented as an alternative that supports rapid recovery. The takeaway is to measure your organization's strategy against these scenarios, and to know that a data protection officer can help with applying the regulations.

talks.title: Macrocell vs. Small Cell vs. Femtocell: 5G Base Stations Compared
talks.teaser: Compares macrocells, small cells and femtocells on size, coverage, cost and how each carries 5G signals.
talks.summary:
This short explainer argues that 5G does not rely on one type of base station. It sets out three kinds and how they differ in size, coverage and cost. Macrocells are large towers, often 50 to 200 feet tall, that cover miles and stand along highways and in rural areas. The video puts the US total at about 200,000, used by carriers such as Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile, with each costing roughly $200,000 to install.

Small cells are roughly the size of a pizza box and cover about a football field's worth of area. They suit dense places such as cities, campuses and arenas, and are often mounted on streetlights or utility poles. Femtocells, about the size of a paperback, provide indoor connectivity in homes and offices. They connect back through the internet, work like routers, and cost about $100. Small cells cost around $10,000.

The main contrast is in signal behaviour. Macrocells use low frequencies that pass through walls and windows. Small cells carry 5G's high-frequency millimeter waves over about 100 yards, but those signals need a clear line of sight and cannot penetrate walls, so even heavy rain can affect them. Femtocells have a short range without the line-of-sight limit. The video notes that earlier generations could use small cells for extra capacity, while 5G's millimeter-wave bands depend on them. It also says full 5G coverage may need five to 10 times more small cells than macrocells, likely not complete until the mid to late 2020s.

talks.title: Network Engineer vs. Software Engineer: What's the Difference?

talks.title: What is VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol)? How Does VoIP Work?
talks.teaser: Explains how VoIP turns an internet connection into a phone line and what it offers businesses and remote workers.
talks.summary:
VoIP, short for Voice over Internet Protocol, lets people make phone calls over an internet connection from a computer, smartphone, tablet or dedicated VoIP handset. The service converts voice audio into digital data using codecs and sends it across the internet. When a call goes to a regular phone number, the signal is converted back into telephone format before it reaches the other person. Many people already use VoIP without noticing, since some office desk phones are VoIP devices and others are softphone apps from providers.

The explainer then covers the benefits for organizations. VoIP brings voice, video and text messaging into one system, so teams do not need several applications to communicate. Other advantages include call recording, custom caller ID, voicemail delivered by email, lower costs than traditional phone bills, support for employees joining meetings from anywhere, and cheap international calling.

The video also points out the drawbacks. VoIP needs a fast connection with enough bandwidth to handle several simultaneous calls alongside regular internet traffic, which matters most in large offices. VoIP phones often lack features such as directory assistance, and emergency calls to 911 and other services may stop working during a power outage. The video closes by noting that VoIP is sometimes confused with IP telephony and inviting viewers to compare the two.

talks.title: What is IaC (Infrastructure as Code)?
talks.teaser: Explains infrastructure as code, how it manages IT resources through software, its benefits and drawbacks, and common tools.
talks.summary:
Infrastructure as code, usually shortened to IaC, is presented as a way to manage IT infrastructure by writing it as software instead of relying on physical hardware. The video recalls that building servers once meant installing and configuring hardware by hand, a process that was expensive, slow and prone to inconsistency. With code-based definitions, operations or development teams can provision and monitor resources automatically, and those files are easy to edit, copy and distribute.

The video stresses that this code needs the same discipline as application software, including version control, testing and staged approval before anything reaches production. Listed advantages are speed over manual setup for databases, networking, user accounts and other services, and consistency, since servers and applications can be deployed to match business policies. Because the configuration passes through the same version control and CI/CD pipelines as application code, it fits with DevOps practice. The drawbacks are a learning curve and the chance of new errors, the risk of configuration drift between devices, and more responsibility on developers to write efficient code.

The talk contrasts two approaches: declarative, which describes the desired end state without the steps to reach it, and imperative, which specifies the commands needed to get there. Common tools named include AWS CloudFormation, Red Hat Ansible, Chef and Puppet. The closing section separates this from scripting, which automates specific static steps, and points viewers to a linked resource on how the two work together in practice.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: Microsoft Keynote
talks.teaser: Shows how synthetic DNA can hold digital archives at extreme density, covering encoding, synthesis, sequencing and decoding.
talks.summary:
Karin Strauss of Microsoft Research argues that the amount of data being generated is outpacing the capacity stored on devices, and that shrinking transistors alone may not close the gap. Her alternative is storing digital information in synthetic DNA, mapping bits onto the four bases. She cites a test tube of dried DNA holding about 10 terabytes, an exabyte that could fit in roughly one cubic inch, and encapsulated DNA that can last a long time. A sustainability comparison with tape for archival storage found lower greenhouse gas, energy and water figures for DNA.

The talk then walked through the pipeline. Data is split into numbered strands with redundancy and tags, synthesized base by base in parallel, then sealed in silica particles. Reading uses sequencing by synthesis or nanopore devices, both producing noisy reads with substitutions, insertions and deletions. Decoding groups reads from the same origin, takes a majority vote, and applies Reed-Solomon error correction. Work to date has stored one gigabyte of information, including a music video and archival music. An automated prototype wrote the word hello into one DNA sequence, and a digital microfluidics board was shown for moving droplets to organize DNA into a library.

Strauss also described an approach to similarity search, where DNA derived from image features binds to matching items, and said archival storage is the first target. She closed by announcing a DNA data storage alliance with Illumina, Twist Biosciences and Western Digital, aimed at education, use cases and a roadmap to commercial deployment.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: IBM Research Keynote
talks.teaser: Shows how analog memory devices can run neural network math in place, trading device challenges for energy and speed gains.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the explosion of data and the rise of deep learning after 2011, when large datasets, internet-scale data and parallel compute came together. It walks through how feedforward, convolutional, recurrent and transformer networks work, and why the largest models now draw heavy energy, with training energy for the biggest models doubling every 3.5 months.

The speaker then contrasts digital accelerators, which cut training to 16-bit floats and inference to 8-bit integers, with analog in-memory computing, where Ohm's law performs the multiplication and Kirchhoff's current law performs the accumulation. For inference, phase change memory is the focus, with retention, programming error and conductance drift as the main challenges. Projected cells, noise-aware training and multiple conductances per weight are presented as ways to address them, and projected cells achieved matrix operations roughly comparable to 8-bit fixed point accuracy.

For training, resistive RAM and ECRAM devices are examined for the symmetric conductance updates that stochastic gradient descent needs. A training approach that exchanges updates between two sets of matrices is shown to converge even with highly asymmetric devices. The talk closes by arguing that analog approaches are a promising complement to digital accelerators, with memory-based architectures for both inference and training still under active development.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: NVM Express Keynote
talks.teaser: Covers how the NVMe specification is being refactored for NVMe 2.0 and where computational storage fits.
talks.summary:
Amber Huffman, Intel's chief technologist of IP engineering and president of NVM Express, opens by describing the widening gap between compute and memory performance. She shows how 3D XPoint, 3D NAND and persistent memory fill the levels between DRAM and flash, and previews a second-generation Optane SSD on PCIe Gen 4 that targets more than double the performance of the first.

She then traces NVMe's growth, from media shipped rising from three petabytes in 2016 to 29 petabytes in 2019, with 54 petabytes projected for 2020. The specification has been refactored into a clean core with separate command set families for block I/O, key-value and zoned namespaces, and independent transports for PCIe, RDMA and TCP. Architectural additions include namespace types, zoned namespaces paired with endurance groups, and domains and partitions for multipath fabric deployments.

The closing section covers computational storage, illustrated by counting New York entries in an encrypted, compressed database table. Instead of moving the whole table to the host, a downloaded, hardware-agnostic program would decrypt, decompress and filter the data on the device. In the Q&A she expects NVMe 2.0 around the end of the first quarter, and computational storage work with SNIA is laying a foundation expected to evolve over the next five years.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: IBM Storage Keynote
talks.teaser: Explains how IBM made QLC flash, the cheapest flash type, endure and perform well enough for primary enterprise storage.
talks.summary:
IBM's vice president of storage development, Alastair Simon, argues that QLC flash, the least expensive flash type on the market, can serve primary enterprise storage. The usual approach is to tier QLC behind TLC, which adds software complexity and can cause performance problems when workloads shift quickly. QLC is harder to use because programming and reads are slower, data retention is weaker, and cells interfere with each other more, all of which reduce endurance.

He describes the second-generation Flash Core Module, a dual-port U.2 NVMe drive built on Micron's 96-layer QLC memory. Its design combines heat isolation and condition-based data placement, inline compression, dynamic switching between SLC and QLC pages, and programming suspension so that reads can get through during long writes. He says the drive reaches two full engine writes per day, and that its error-correction algorithm handles bit error rates ten times higher than standard SSDs. Capacities run from 4.8 TB to 38.4 TB, and a 24-drive FS9000 reaches 757 TB of usable capacity. Compared with the earlier TLC-based module, he reports 44% higher read productivity, 33% higher write productivity, and lower response times.

The talk closes with two related trends. Computational storage moves tasks such as compression from the host CPU into the SSD, and the speaker notes that SNIA has a working group on it. Persistent memory, or storage-class memory, is presented as a cheaper alternative to DRAM for read caching, which could also remove the need for batteries in storage controllers. The main takeaway is that cheaper flash can handle primary workloads when the drive itself manages placement and wear.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: Intel Keynote
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Flash Memory Summit 2020: Intel Keynote.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Intel's 2020 Flash Memory Summit keynote presents a one-year progress update on Optane persistent memory technology. The speaker addresses the critical memory bottleneck facing modern data centers: while CPU core counts on Xeon processors have grown exponentially through architectural innovations like chiplets, DRAM scaling has dramatically slowed from 4x density increases every three years (mid-1990s) to only 2x density every four years currently, with per-bit cost declining even more slowly at roughly 10-12% annually. This creates an unsustainable gap between compute demand and memory capacity that aligns with Amdahl's Law—memory must scale proportionally with compute power.

## Solution Architecture

Intel's response is a re-architected two-tiered memory and storage hierarchy. For memory, this pairs a performance tier (DRAM accessed via standard cache/memory hierarchies) with a capacity tier (Optane persistent memory attached to the DDR bus, accessed through load/store instructions at near-DRAM speeds but significantly cheaper than DRAM). For storage, Optane serves as a high-performance non-volatile tier while traditional SSDs provide cost-effective capacity, enabling both performance and cost objectives simultaneously.

## Ecosystem and Market Adoption

Over one year, Intel developed a robust ecosystem spanning all major OEMs, systems integrators, cloud service providers, and ISVs with qualified and optimized software. Market adoption significantly exceeded typical new product performance: approximately 200 Fortune 500 companies have deployed persistent memory or are in proof-of-concept stages, with an 85% POC-to-deployment conversion rate, resulting in over 270 production installations. Customer deployments fall into three benefit categories: TCO savings (30-40% system cost reduction through DRAM replacement without performance loss), throughput improvements (2-4x job increases by eliminating memory bottlenecks), and faster time-to-insights (order-of-magnitude improvements via persistent storage features and instantaneous recovery).

## Second Generation Performance

Intel released the 200 series persistent memory with a new media controller delivering 25% performance improvement over first generation. Benchmark comparisons show dramatic advantages: 1000x lower latency versus NVMe SSDs at 1GB/s traffic, 3.8x higher bandwidth than SSDs, and sustained performance under heavy load.

## Customer Deployments and Applications

SAP HANA testing demonstrated compelling value: doubling system memory capacity while maintaining similar DRAM-level costs, with 6x faster database restart times; alternatively, reducing server counts by 50% for large databases while maintaining capacity and achieving 52% lower hardware costs. The DAOS (Distributed Asynchronous Object Store) software stack, co-developed with HPC customers, combines persistent memory with traditional storage by placing small, frequently accessed metadata and indices on persistent memory while aligning larger data structures to block storage. This eliminates serialization overhead and block contention from concurrent multi-process access. DAOS achieved record results on the IO 500 storage benchmark, scoring 2x the next solution overall and claiming the top three positions (Intel DAOS, Texas Advanced Computing Center, and Argonne National Labs) in the 10-node challenge.

Oracle Exadata X8M exemplifies deep collaboration, integrating persistent memory with RDMA over converged ethernet for the hot storage tier. Results include 2.5x higher IOPS (16 million total), 10x better latency (under 19 microseconds for database reads), and availability on Oracle Cloud as a competitive advantage. RDMA-based replication to persistent memory demonstrated 10x+ latency improvements compared to NVMe SSDs over TCP.

## Developer Resources and RDMA Democratization

Intel released libRPMA libraries within PMDK (Persistent Memory Developer Kit) to democratize RDMA integration, enabling developers to use popular APIs without rewriting applications. The speaker highlights the free "Programming Persistent Memory" book and online resources. The keynote emphasizes collaborative innovation and thanks ecosystem partners, customers, and audience contributors to the persistent memory revolution.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: Xilinx Keynote
talks.teaser: Surveys how FPGA-based smart NICs, computational storage and CXL are reshaping data center architecture and confidential computing.
talks.summary:
This Flash Memory Summit keynote, delivered in a remote format in 2020, starts with three industry trends the speaker says will shape the data center: compute gains that now depend on specialized hardware as clock speeds plateau, a sharp rise in bus and link bandwidth from PCIe and CXL, and the spread of hybrid and distributed cloud designs.

The middle of the talk gives concrete examples of moving processing close to the data. In a virtualized server, the host CPU spends cycles on virtual switch lookups for every packet. The speaker shows an FPGA-based smart NIC that handles those lookups in the card at line rate, and notes that customers can add custom rules without slowing the server. For storage, computational storage puts processing inside the drive so data does not have to cross to the CPU. The speaker mentions a joint Samsung and Xilinx computational storage drive that completed qualification, and describes a regular expression search appliance built from many such drives, with one government forensics customer reportedly cutting search time from hours to seconds. The talk also covers memory disaggregation, where storage class memory and CXL lower latency enough to pool memory across a fabric.

The closing section turns to security. As cloud management software extends onto customer-owned hardware, physical protection can no longer be assumed, so the speaker argues every link needs trusted connections. He points to hardware roots of trust, random number generators, key management and physically unclonable functions as building blocks for confidential computing. The keynote ends by calling security a first design principle, and a Q&A answer explains why FPGAs suit computational storage: their reconfigurable fabric and programmable I/O can fetch data directly from storage.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: NVIDIA Keynote
talks.teaser: Explains how NVIDIA plans to remove storage I/O bottlenecks for AI using RDMA, Magnum IO, and BlueField DPUs.
talks.summary:
The keynote starts from the idea that AI depends on data access, since larger GPU compute and larger datasets both put pressure on storage. Once GPUs take over the compute-heavy part of a workload, the time spent computing shrinks and storage I/O becomes the bottleneck. Modern sharded and streaming applications add more east-west traffic between servers, which strains the data center network further.

NVIDIA presented Magnum IO, its software platform for moving data between GPUs across and within servers and from GPUs to external storage, with RDMA as the underlying technology. The speakers asked the storage community to adopt RDMA and Magnum IO and to build high-performance storage at scale rather than trading performance against capacity. They then introduced the BlueField DPU for offloading I/O work. Figures given for BlueField 2 included almost 7 billion transistors, 100 gigabits per second of IPsec, over five million NVMe IOPS, and work that would take more than 125 CPU cores in software.

The DOCA software platform runs software-defined storage, networking, security, and management on the DPU for virtual machines and containers, freeing CPU cores for applications. NVIDIA said existing VMware and Linux setups would not need changes, and that DOCA would carry over to BlueField 2X, which pairs the DPU with an Ampere GPU. Partners were named for validated systems, GPUDirect Storage, and EGX and HGX building blocks. The talk ended with a call for more OEMs and storage vendors to join, followed by a live Q&A.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: Fungible Keynote

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: Marvell Keynote
talks.teaser: Shows how Marvell accelerators and Ethernet SSD converters offload host CPUs to scale NVMe flash storage.
talks.summary:
This Flash Memory Summit 2020 keynote, given remotely by a marketing lead at Marvell's flash business unit, argued that NVMe flash has outrun the server processors meant to drive it. Faster PCIe generations and denser NAND leave host CPUs as the bottleneck, so the presenter made the case for hardware accelerators that take storage work off the processor.

Two accelerator examples came first. A low-power PCIe card handles RAID 1 boot files for an HPE server, keeping boot data separate from the main user RAID stripe. Another function offloads storage I/O virtualization from the hypervisor so virtual machines can reach SSDs directly in multi-tenant environments.

The later sections moved to NVMe over Fabrics. JBOF boxes are limited by their NIC and CPU, so Marvell showed a converter that translates NVMe-oF to NVMe at the drive, and an Ethernet bunch-of-flash platform built on two Marvell switches. Los Alamos and Micron benchmarks, the latter run on an Nvidia DGX A100, showed better scaling and a fourfold storage throughput gain. The talk closed with client, edge and automotive controller work, with the message that offloading the host and converging networking with storage is how NVMe scales.

talks.title: AI vs. Data Science: Differences in Technology and Use Cases
talks.teaser: Explains how data science and AI differ in methods, data needs and business use, and how they combine in practice.
talks.summary:
This short explainer from Eye on Tech, presented by Jamison Cush, addresses a common point of confusion: how AI and data science differ, even though businesses often use them together. The video frames both as technology sets that overlap in enterprise settings while serving different purposes.

Data science is described as a discipline built on statistics and algorithms, used to examine large volumes of information and draw out business insight, for example by building recommendation engines or forecasting user behavior. AI is presented as a machine's capacity to interpret data, learn from it and act on it in a human-like way. The speaker notes that current AI is narrow, trained on large amounts of data for specific tasks, and that this training approach is machine learning. Data science can work with varied data types because people stay involved in shaping the analysis, whereas AI typically needs clean, labelled datasets that its algorithms process on their own.

The video then sketches a combined workflow. A data scientist first uses data science to learn how a business process works, where it could improve and which errors recur, then brings in AI to streamline or automate that process. The closing point is that machine learning is only one tool for generating insights, and viewers are pointed to a companion piece on 15 common data science techniques.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: WD Keynote
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Flash Memory Summit 2020: WD Keynote.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: Numem Keynote
talks.teaser: MRAM-backed DNN accelerators enable onboard spacecraft AI when slow Earth links make cloud analytics impractical.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with the scale of global data growth, arguing that piping everything to the cloud breaks down for space missions where round-trip links can exceed twenty minutes, bandwidth is scarce, and bidirectional traffic raises security exposure. NASA’s answer is distributed intelligence at sensors, rovers, and spacecraft, with strict size, weight, and power goals plus needs for retention through power loss, wide temperature, high endurance, radiation tolerance, and fast local inference.

Magnetoresistive RAM is positioned as the enabler: much lower standby power than alternatives, non-volatility for code and coefficients, strong endurance in testing, and encouraging early radiation screening with no observed failures in preliminary mil-style exercises. A scalable partner accelerator scales processing elements and daisy-chains chips toward high TOPS, splitting SRAM for streaming activations and MRAM for weights with flow control. Customer examples cite slashing external DRAM traffic from about 32 gigabytes per second to roughly 2.7 gigabytes per second, with large idle-memory power savings.

Software stacks on CUDA-compatible tooling and common deep-learning libraries, with benchmarks against NVIDIA Jetson-class parts showing roughly double image throughput and better images-per-watt in demanding modes. Representative space workloads include sensor fusion, terrain mapping, and navigation models. Practitioners should treat edge AI plus non-volatile on-chip memory as the practical path to autonomy when Earth is far away, while planning further radiation qualification beyond first-pass lab results.

talks.title: Flash Memory Summit 2020: IDC Keynote
talks.teaser: Maps how the pandemic reshaped digital transformation, cloud adoption and edge infrastructure plans, using IDC market data.
talks.summary:
Matt Eastwood, who manages IDC's IoT research team, frames the pandemic as a wake-up call that pushed organizations to speed up digital transformation. He cites a survey in which over a third of tech decision makers had further accelerated their efforts, and a maturity model showing only about 35 percent of organizations were digitally transformed before the crisis. The C-suite's agenda items were also reordered, with resiliency, customer experience and connectivity moving to the top.

The middle of the talk looks at spending and infrastructure. Organizations moved from business continuity toward cost optimization, with about 75 percent of pre-COVID IT roadmaps still in place. Eastwood argues that cloud is an operating model rather than a destination, and that only about half of organizations have run a production workload in public cloud. Technology resiliency rated weakest among the resiliency areas, and he expects edge locations to hold more than half of new infrastructure, up from about 10 percent today.

He closes with predictions: microservices in 80 percent of new workloads, purpose-built coprocessors and accelerators, and more than 75 percent of edge infrastructure consumed as a service. For practitioners, the takeaway is to plan infrastructure for hybrid, multi-cloud and edge placement, prioritise agility and resiliency, and expect service providers to take on capacity and risk.

talks.title: 3 Necessary Skills for Network Automation
talks.teaser: Outlines three starting skills that help network engineers move from manual device work into network automation.
talks.summary:
The video argues that networking is becoming more software dependent, so network engineers and managers should learn network automation to keep up. It presents this as an ongoing process that does not require strong programming skills to begin.

The first skill is non-technical. Engineers are encouraged to change their mindset, consider automating routine work such as configuration, monitoring and troubleshooting, and accept that adoption takes short-term investment for long-term gains. Automation can start with existing features such as configuration validation and update functions. The second skill is scripting without full programming. Ansible is suggested for running commands and collecting output, validating network operations, generating configurations from templates and loading them onto devices. Learners are also advised to use a web-based source code repository to test and store their scripts.

The third skill is basic software knowledge, including terminology and concepts such as refactoring, iteration, loops, conditionals and lists, which helps when working with developers. The next step is development itself, with Python named as the main language for network automation. Free or low-cost resources are available, or an engineer can pair program with a developer who is learning networking. The video closes by stressing that networking keeps changing, so lifelong learning matters, and it mentions that a network automation certificate can add to skills and credibility.

talks.title: What is Multifactor Authentication (MFA)?
talks.teaser: Explains how multifactor authentication combines credential types like passwords, devices and biometrics to block unauthorized logins.
talks.summary:
Passwords alone are a weak defense because they can be guessed, forgotten or reused across many services. The video introduces multifactor authentication, or MFA, as a login process that requires more than one form of verification. It notes that many security experts prefer the term multi-factor over two-factor for any scheme that uses more than one credential. Each added layer means that an attacker who compromises one factor still faces another barrier before reaching the target.

The presenter walks through five categories of factors. Knowledge factors are things a user knows, such as a password or security question. Possession factors are physical items like a security token or an authorized phone app. Inherence factors are biological traits such as fingerprints, facial recognition or voice. Location factors rely on signals like GPS from a smartphone. Time factors restrict access to certain hours, such as checking an employee's login against their work schedule to stop off-hours account hijacking. An everyday example is paying at a gas station by swiping a card and then entering a ZIP code.

The video argues that MFA matters to businesses of every kind, given the growth of SaaS services and widespread password reuse. It closes by suggesting viewers learn what they need to know before buying an MFA tool, and it asks viewers to share enterprise and consumer use cases in the comments.

talks.title: What is Data Science? What Does a Data Scientist Do?
talks.teaser: Explains what data science involves, what data scientists do, and why organizations are hiring for the role.
talks.summary:
Data science is presented as the practice of applying advanced analytics to large datasets to pull out information that guides business operations and strategy. The video says it affects costs, efficiency, marketing and sales, and can give a company an edge over rivals. A data scientist usually comes from mathematics, statistics or computer science, and also needs enough business sense and communication skill to explain findings to senior executives.

The role relies on techniques such as machine learning, predictive modeling, data mining, data preparation and visualization. A bank trying to understand why it is losing customers is used as an example: the scientist decides which data and methods fit the question, then carries out the analysis. Other examples include customer-facing firms refining target audiences, recruiters building aptitude tests to improve hiring, streaming services shaping programming and recommendations, and shipping companies optimizing routes and transport modes.

The speaker says demand is rising as organizations generate more data, with the data science platform market projected to grow above 20% a year over five years, while qualified workers remain scarce. One suggested response is to train people from software engineering, business analysis or the physical sciences in data science as a long-term investment. The video closes by pointing viewers to further material on how enterprises can adapt to the shortage.

talks.title: 10 Things to Look for in a Colocation Provider
talks.teaser: Ten factors to weigh when picking a colocation provider, covering power, location, contracts, fees, compliance, security and services.
talks.summary:
Colocation means renting space in a data center for your own servers and hardware, usually with power, cooling and physical security included, and sometimes with networking or management services. The talk argues that choosing the right provider is what lets a business capture those benefits, and it walks through ten things to check before committing.

Power and space come first. The provider must be able to deliver the power a business actually needs, since power-hungry equipment can bring a significant surcharge, while consolidating racks into a smaller footprint can cut costs. Connectivity matters too: a provider that supports several network carriers gives better pricing and allows redundant links. Location should be close enough for access yet far enough from fire, flood or storm risk. Contract terms, including the master service agreement and service level agreement, should be reviewed with legal and IT teams and negotiated for better terms.

The speaker also flags costs that are harder to see, such as setup, connectivity changes, and backup or data protection add-ons. Compliance means confirming that the claimed tier certifications are real, since some workloads depend on them. Security measures should be checked, including options like cameras on the floor. Managed services such as backup, disaster recovery planning and testing, and remote staff support should be available. Finally, the talk recommends discussing the provider's roadmap and how the contract can change over time, because a business is not bound to one provider for life.

talks.title: WLAN vs. Wi-Fi: What's the Difference?
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for WLAN vs. Wi-Fi: What's the Difference?.

talks.title: 9 Best Practices for VDI Storage
talks.teaser: Nine practical guidelines cover user patterns, encryption, platform choice, and disaster recovery for virtual desktop storage.
talks.summary:
Virtual desktop environments depend on physical storage backends, and sizing and securing that layer is a common pain point for administrators. The presentation frames nine practices meant to reduce guesswork when planning capacity, performance, and resilience for VDI.

The guidance starts with understanding users: which applications they run, how demand fluctuates, required IOPS, and stored data volume. Security advice emphasizes least privilege on resources, encryption, and endpoint protections. It then walks through storage for separate VDI building blocks such as access managers, license servers, and hypervisors; choosing platforms sized for the deployment instead of legacy gear; and shifting from HDDs toward SSDs or hybrid tiered designs. Supporting technologies include RAID, software-defined storage, local caching, and ongoing monitoring. Product-level efficiencies cover linked clones, thin provisioning, disaster recovery via replication or database failover clusters, and multi-site or cloud-backed designs for distributed remote workers.

Practitioners are urged to treat VDI storage as a planned system rather than an afterthought. The close points to storage class memory and other emerging options as further ways to improve VDI storage outcomes.

talks.title: Talent Management vs. Talent Acquisition vs. Recruitment
talks.teaser: Explains how talent management, talent acquisition and recruitment differ in scope, timeline and purpose.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why three commonly confused HR terms describe separate processes, each with its own team and purpose. Talent management is the broadest of the three. It covers how employees are handled across their working life at a company, typically through systems for recruitment and onboarding, learning and development, performance, compensation and succession planning.

Talent acquisition sits inside that umbrella as a more strategic, forward-looking effort. Rather than only filling vacancies, it builds long-term plans for future roles, cultivates sources of candidates for key positions, and aims to secure quality hires and clear career paths. The speaker argues this reduces business risk by cutting the time and money lost to constant turnover. Recruitment is also part of talent management and overlaps with acquisition, but it concentrates on the present, trying to fill open roles as quickly as possible in a reactive, linear way.

The closing contrast is that recruitment responds to immediate gaps, while talent acquisition is proactive and cyclical, building a pipeline ahead of need. The talk ends by pointing to AI as a way to strengthen talent acquisition, from sourcing through interviewing, and invites viewers to share how their organizations approach it.

talks.title: What is API Testing and Why is it Important?
talks.teaser: Explains what API testing is, the main test types used, and why it helps connected software work reliably.
talks.summary:
The video introduces the application programming interface, the code that lets two software programs communicate, using the example of a button that shares content from a website to a social network. It explains that APIs need testing to confirm they work as intended, stay secure, perform well and remain reliable. A typical API test sends requests to one or more endpoints and compares the responses with the results that were expected.

The talk then walks through the main categories of API testing. Validation testing checks the product's behavior and efficiency, while functional testing confirms the API does exactly what it should. Load testing measures how many calls an API can handle, and reliability testing checks that it returns consistent results. Security testing examines encryption and access control, penetration testing looks at attack vectors from an outside view, and fuzz testing feeds in large volumes of data to try to trigger a crash or overflow.

The speaker argues that testing can begin early in development, before the user interface exists, and that catching bugs at this stage can remove at least half of them before they grow into serious problems, which saves money later. An example is a service that offers login through another provider, which needs testing to confirm the two platforms exchange information securely. The video closes by noting that API testing differs from web services testing and points viewers to a linked resource on that difference.

talks.title: What is a Software-Defined Perimeter (SDP)?
talks.teaser: Explains how software-defined perimeters cloak network resources and grant access based on identity and least privilege.
talks.summary:
Traditional enterprise networks separate their internal systems from the outside world with fixed boundaries such as firewalls. The video argues that these boundaries fall short against phishing, untrusted access inside the perimeter, and the extension of the perimeter onto the internet. A software-defined perimeter, or SDP, builds that boundary in software rather than hardware and keeps an organization's infrastructure hidden from outsiders. The presenter notes that this approach is sometimes called a black cloud, because it cloaks systems behind the virtual boundary.

An SDP ties access to identity. It authenticates and authorizes users and endpoints before connecting them to isolated services, and it applies least privilege so each person receives only the access their task requires. The talk lists several network threats that SDPs reduce, including denial of service, man-in-the-middle and brute force attacks, port scanning, server vulnerabilities and lateral movement. Other benefits mentioned include support for many device types, restricted broad network access, risk-based policy, control over services and applications, isolation of mission-critical data, and protection for hybrid and private clouds.

The presenter also describes using SDP tools alongside VPNs, which are prone to credential theft and excessive access. An SDP can create micro perimeters for fine-grained user access. The talk further explains that SDP and zero trust can be deployed together, with SDP cloaking the network and its resources while zero trust keeps authentication checks in place. The closing prompt asks viewers which benefits an SDP would bring to their own organization and points to further comparison of SDP, VPN and zero-trust networks.

talks.title: What is a Microsoft Technology Associate (MTA) Certification?
talks.teaser: Explains Microsoft's entry-level MTA certification path, its exam collections, and the careers each can support.
talks.summary:
The video introduces Microsoft Technology Associate (MTA), a set of entry-level certifications meant to build core technology knowledge for people starting out. Microsoft aims the program at beginners, IT generalists and students who do not yet have job experience in a specialty. Candidates must pass at least one of twelve exams, and the lineup covers foundational subjects such as programming in Java, building HTML5 apps and Windows operating system topics.

The presenter explains that the exams are grouped into three recommended collections based on the career a person wants: IT infrastructure, covering server, private cloud and desktop roles; database, covering business intelligence and database administration; and developer, covering software development. A learner can take a single exam to earn certification in one topic, or work through a full collection. The credential adds credibility for people with limited IT experience, although the tests assume some hands-on practice or training. Preparation options include Microsoft's free online course or a paid instructor-led program.

The closing part lists job roles the credential can support, including network architect, helpdesk technician, software engineer, mobile app developer, database administrator and website developer. Viewers are pointed to Azure certifications aimed at IT administrators if they want to explore other Microsoft credentials.

talks.title: CDP vs. DMP: Differences in Data Sources and Use Cases
talks.teaser: Explains how customer data platforms and data management platforms differ in data sources, lifespan and use cases.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why customer data platforms (CDPs) and data management platforms (DMPs) are often confused. Both collect and organize customer information and sound alike, yet they serve different purposes. A CDP gathers a company's own first-party data, such as website activity, CRM records, social profiles, feedback and subscription emails, then merges records that belong to the same person into one profile that any department can use. A DMP is typically a warehouse of anonymized data drawn mostly from web, mobile and advertising sources, and it centers on purchased second- and third-party data.

The presenter contrasts how long the data lasts and how complete it is. CDP data is kept long term and supports faster internal decisions, real-time recommendations and personalized service. Bought data is described as short-lived, less complete and harder to keep compliant with privacy rules. DMPs gather information on prospective buyers, including cookie and device identifiers, and feed ad technology platforms that reach those people online.

The talk closes by noting that a CDP differs from marketing automation, and it points viewers to further material on how the tools differ. The practical takeaway is that a DMP is aimed at reaching new prospects while a CDP serves existing customers, even though the two overlap in some features.

talks.title: WhatIs.com Virtual Book Club: The Phoenix Project, Chapters 5, 6, & 7
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss chapters 5 to 7 of The Phoenix Project, covering compliance pressure, silos and bottlenecks in DevOps.
talks.summary:
This episode of WhatIs.com's virtual book club is a panel of technical writers reviewing chapters 5 through 7 of The Phoenix Project, a business novel about DevOps. The story's company, Parts Unlimited, starts to feel the strain of its IT problems. A compliance audit report lists a heavy load of IT concerns, and the chief information officer is criticized for not giving controls enough attention while colleagues avoid him. The panel asks whether his stress and the information silos around him come from his personality or from his job. Along the way they explain terms such as personally identifiable information and the role of the CISO.

The conversation then turns to bottlenecks. Brent is the one person who knows how to fix things, so he is pulled into every request and slows down the release that matters most to the business. One panelist connects this to the Theory of Constraints, which holds that a whole system can only move as fast as its slowest step. The group also notes that the authors draw parallels between IT and a manufacturing plant, and they expect the lean production ideas shown on a factory tour to carry over into IT.

The host closes with a short summary of the Three Ways: workflow, feedback loops, and a culture where people feel safe experimenting and learning from failure. The panel guesses that lean production will be the key term for chapter eight. Listeners are pointed to free study resources on WhatIs.com.

talks.title: 8 Characteristics of Cloud Computing
talks.teaser: Breaks down eight defining traits of cloud computing, from on-demand provisioning and pooling to elasticity and broad access.
talks.summary:
Cloud computing began as an alternative to on-premises storage, but the label now covers software as a service, AI, networking and business applications. This short video asks what actually separates genuine cloud services from everything marketed as cloud, and answers with eight characteristics.

The first traits concern how capacity is consumed. Developers can provision the tools they need themselves through a self-service portal, and providers serve many customers from shared, multi-tenant architectures. Compute, storage and networking can be added or removed as demand changes, allowing systems to scale vertically or horizontally. Billing follows usage, so customers pay only for the virtual machines, storage, processing or bandwidth they consume, and some providers bill by the second. Measured service tracks consumption on both sides, which supports billing and shows providers how customers use their resources.

The remaining traits cover reliability, security and reach. Providers use a range of techniques to prevent downtime, and workloads can be spread across availability zones and redundant network connections. Because public providers share underlying infrastructure, they rely on strong isolation between workloads, strict access rights, data encryption and identity and access management. Finally, data can be reached from any location with internet access. The video closes by noting that real benefits depend on a sound strategy to avoid cost pitfalls, and points viewers to a separate video on five ways to reduce cloud costs.

talks.title: What is an IoT Gateway and Why is it Important?
talks.teaser: Explains how IoT gateways translate device protocols, filter sensor data at the edge, and manage connected devices.
talks.summary:
This short explainer covers what an IoT gateway is and why connected devices depend on one. The gateway is described as a point of entry and exit for network data, similar to a traditional network gateway. It sits between edge equipment such as sensors and controllers and external networks like the cloud, translating the many protocols those devices use, including Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, MQTT and serial connections.

The middle of the video focuses on processing data at the edge. As the number of connected sensors grows, so does the volume of data they produce, so a gateway can drop routine readings and forward only unusual or critical ones. An office building with thousands of sensors is used as an example: the gateway would send temperature data to the cloud only when it falls outside a set range. Beyond translation and filtering, gateways handle connectivity, security, updates and management. Some newer models can also run code that analyzes data and takes action, such as switching on air conditioning when a room becomes too hot.

The takeaway is that a gateway lets an organization handle large volumes of device data locally, reducing what reaches the cloud while keeping its connected devices managed and secure.

talks.title: What is Deepfake AI? Deepfake Content and Elections
talks.teaser: Explains what deepfakes are, how generator and discriminator networks create them, and why they threaten elections.
talks.summary:
Sabrina Polin introduces deepfakes as a form of artificial intelligence that produces convincing fake images, audio, and video. The name blends deep learning with fake, and it refers both to the underlying technology and to the doctored content it creates. She notes that deepfakes now appear across many industries, from politics to IT security.

The explanation then covers how deepfakes are built. Two AI models, a generator and a discriminator, work against each other in a generative adversarial network. The generator produces forged footage, such as placing a politician's face on another person's body, while the discriminator judges whether content is real. Each side improves in response to the other, which yields a believable result. Video was once harder to alter than photos or audio, but deepfake tools put that ability within reach of almost anyone. Malicious actors can then make people appear to say or do things they never did, usually to damage reputations or spread falsehoods.

The main concern is election manipulation. Deepfakes can distort reality and could sway voters when aimed at a political candidate. Polin says experts think deepfakes of public figures are unlikely to go unrecognized for long, but they can still cause harm if they are not caught in time. Voters, political institutions, law enforcement, and IT professionals should all watch for the threat, and IT leaders are urged to understand the security risks involved. The video closes by asking viewers whether they have ever spotted a deepfake and what gave it away.

talks.title: Thick vs. Thin Clients: Comparing VDI Hardware
talks.teaser: Explains the differences between thick, thin and zero clients, weighing their security, cost and management trade-offs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining the two main computing models. A thick client, sometimes called a fat client, keeps most of its resources on a local physical device, so staff can work offline and users can customize the software and settings. The speaker notes that company laptops are usually thick clients. Their drawbacks are weaker security, since the device holds all of a person's data, the need for backups, higher upfront and maintenance costs, and the fact that new applications must be installed on each workstation separately.

The second half covers thin clients, sometimes called lean clients, which run as virtual desktops with data and applications kept on a central server. Shared public machines such as those in government offices and libraries are typical examples, with each person signing in individually. The speaker argues that this arrangement is more secure, resists malware better, has longer life cycles, uses less power, costs less to buy, is easier to manage and scales more readily. The downsides are a dependence on a constant network connection, slower performance than local computing, bandwidth and performance bottlenecks, and the requirement to plan server capacity for the number of users.

The talk closes by pointing out that not every device fits neatly into either category. It also mentions zero clients, or ultra-thin clients, which have no local storage at all. The speaker finishes by asking viewers whether their own computer is a thick or thin client and how they could tell.

talks.title: 7 Election Technology Use Cases
talks.teaser: Surveys technology's role across elections, from voter databases and voting machines to deepfakes and result checks.
talks.summary:
Sabrina Polin walks through the ways technology is used before, during and after an election, with the goal of showing both its helpful and harmful sides. She starts with the infrastructure that makes voting possible, including registered voter databases, ballot data files, servers, storage and networks. She then covers campaigns, describing candidates' social media outreach and voter-information apps that match people with candidates based on platform issues. She also mentions a Microsoft service that detects cyber attacks against people tied to campaigns and offers remediation help.

The talk then turns to misuse. Robocalls and automated texts that carry false information about election days or changed polling sites can mislead voters. AI-generated deepfake videos can make candidates look bad and spread false voting details. On the voting side, she explains that some places use electronic machines or computers, while paper ballots are typically optical scan ballots that machines read. Casting and counting can involve recording, encrypting, transmitting and tabulating votes. When a voting method cannot be trusted, technology can help check results. She cites a Microsoft tool that lets voters confirm their votes were accounted for, and statistical and pattern analysis that can flag suspicious voting patterns.

She closes by saying technology can support turnout and help safeguard elections, but it cannot always stop misinformation from reaching voters. Viewers are pointed to the vulnerability disclosure program of Election Systems & Software, a voting equipment vendor, as a place to learn more.

talks.title: What is an AWS Architecture and How To Develop One
talks.teaser: Introduces AWS storage, compute and networking basics, with live console demos of S3 buckets, EC2 instances and VPC subnets.
talks.summary:
This webinar introduces the building blocks of an IT architecture on Amazon Web Services. The speaker contrasts on-premises work, where capacity planning, buying hardware and waiting weeks for delivery slow teams down, with the cloud, where the provider handles the hardware and resources can be started and stopped within minutes. He argues that costs can follow real demand when the infrastructure is designed well.

The session centers on three areas: storage, compute and networking. For storage, he presents Amazon S3 as pay-per-use object storage with built-in redundancy, then demonstrates creating a bucket, uploading a file and enabling encryption. He shows that objects stay private by default even though each gets a web address, and that making one public takes several deliberate steps. For compute, he covers EC2 virtual machines, horizontal scaling behind a load balancer and disposable servers, and launches an instance whose startup script installs a web server.

For networking, he explains a virtual private cloud as a private network in a chosen region, divided into subnets across availability zones, and walks through a wizard and a manual subnet build. He notes that routing table entries are required before traffic flows. His closing message is that the cloud removes much of the hardware work, but security and design remain the customer's responsibility.

talks.title: What is Edge Computing and its Impact on 5G?
talks.teaser: Explains edge computing as data processing near its source, and why it matters for IoT and 5G networks.
talks.summary:
Edge computing moves data processing to the outer edge of a network, close to where the data is produced, in contrast to a centralized cloud model. The speaker uses two examples to show why distance matters. A smart speaker command usually goes to the cloud and back, which causes a noticeable delay, while the same lag in a self-driving car could be fatal. In an enterprise, placing computing power near routers, wide area network devices and IoT devices means data travels a shorter distance and can reach more processing points.

Edge devices also ease strain on resources by handling data locally and sending only what matters to a remote data center. A smart thermostat transmits only when the temperature moves outside set limits, and a security camera transmits only when it detects motion. The stated benefits include faster time to action, response times down to milliseconds, conserved network capacity and fewer data bottlenecks.

The talk also covers the drawbacks. A distributed design creates more possible attack vectors, licensing costs can erase the low initial price, and administrators may accidentally open security holes or cause configuration drift across many devices. Edge computing is not expected to replace cloud computing. The trend is driven largely by the growth of IoT, and it is needed for 5G, which depends on many network nodes using weaker frequency bands that cover only short distances.

talks.title: AI Cybersecurity Readiness and Challenges
talks.teaser: Argues AI security tools should augment analysts, and that training and explainability decide whether deployments succeed.
talks.summary:
Jessica Groopman, founder and analyst at Kaleido Insights, argues that organisations increasingly turn to AI to spot and counter fast-moving threats, but that these tools are meant to help staff rather than replace them. Autonomous AI agents are not running security operations centers today. Instead, the tools are being placed in the hands of analysts, and augmenting analyst work is the most common starting point she sees.

Looking ahead, she highlights AI-driven pattern detection, such as spotting unusual user behaviour or new attack types, as increasingly important while the number of endpoints keeps growing. She also warns that adversaries are adopting the same technology, and that their techniques, especially when paired with social engineering, should not be underestimated. Successful deployment depends on skills. Analysts need training to use AI for triaging and prioritising alerts, and that education should reach the wider workforce, since any threat landscape is only as strong as its weakest node.

Groopman also raises explainability: analysts must be able to say why a model made a recommendation or assigned a score, not just report the suspicious pattern it found. She closes by noting that AI in security is still early and its long-term implications remain unclear, so training, clear communication and caution are the keys to a secure rollout.

talks.title: WhatIs.com Virtual Book Club: The Phoenix Project, Chapters 3 & 4
talks.teaser: Technical writers discuss chapters three and four of The Phoenix Project, linking each reading to a glossary-style definition.
talks.summary:
This episode of the WhatIs.com virtual book club, hosted by Wes Chai, brings together several technical writers to discuss chapters three and four of The Phoenix Project, a novel about DevOps. The chapters follow the investigation into a payroll outage, where the characters try to work out which change caused it. Each panelist picks a term from the glossary and ties it to events in the reading.

One panelist chooses cognitive bias, admitting to assuming that a developer named Max was a man, a mistake the book also makes. The panelist connects this to a classic riddle about a doctor who turns out to be the patient's mother. Another picks cowboy coding, describing developers editing code directly on a live production server without checks, and links it to weak change management that makes root causes hard to trace.

Other picks cover employee productivity, which the speaker ties to poor collaboration between departments and a manager's order to attend change meetings, and corporate theater, describing an emergency meeting where an executive blames IT operations while performing for the CEO. The discussion closes on the idea that the outage reveals a dysfunctional organization. The panelists note that the protagonist ends the reading concluding that his managers seem to be at war with each other.

talks.title: Type 1 vs. Type 2 Hypervisors: What's the Difference?
talks.teaser: Compares type 1 and type 2 hypervisors and walks through installing Ubuntu in Oracle VirtualBox on a Windows host.
talks.summary:
This instructor-led session explains what a hypervisor does and how it lets one host machine run several operating systems at once as separate virtual machines. It covers the resources each virtual machine consumes, including CPU cores, memory, disk image files and the virtual switch that connects machines, and how the virtual network can be bridged to the physical network outside the host.

The talk then compares the two main hypervisor types. Type 1, or bare-metal, hypervisors such as VMware ESXi and Oracle VM Server run directly on the hardware, which makes them more efficient and able to host more machines, but they are harder to set up and usually need a management console. Type 2, or hosted, hypervisors such as VMware Workstation, VirtualBox and Parallels install on an existing Windows, macOS or Linux desktop. They are easier to deploy but share resources with the host operating system, and a crash of the host takes down every virtual machine on it. The speaker also lists the general benefits of virtualization, including isolation between workloads, simpler backup and migration, and lower energy, cooling and rack space use. The drawbacks are that one failing host affects all of its machines, that anyone with host access reaches every virtual machine, and that each machine still needs its own patching and antivirus.

The session ends with a demonstration of installing Oracle VirtualBox on Windows 10 and creating a virtual machine with 2 GB of memory and a 50 GB dynamically sized disk. The speaker boots it from an Ubuntu ISO, completes the installation and shows Ubuntu running alongside Windows. The closing advice is to virtualize only when it fits real needs rather than because it is a buzzword, and to note that running macOS in VirtualBox is supported only on Apple hardware and requires its own license.

talks.title: How to Set Up Windows Virtual Desktop
talks.teaser: Walks through building a pooled Windows Virtual Desktop environment in Azure Resource Manager and managing its users and sessions.
talks.summary:
This walkthrough shows how to set up a Windows Virtual Desktop environment with Azure Resource Manager, the version of the service that had become generally available that spring. It starts with signing in to Azure, where a free trial account can be used to try the service, and then creating a host pool. The key choices covered are whether the pool is a validation environment, whether it is personal (one user per machine) or pooled (shared multi-session machines), the maximum session limit per host, and the breadth-first or depth-first load balancing method. The presenter notes that session limits should be set per VM size and workload, because too many users hurt performance while too few mean more VMs and higher cost.

Next, session host virtual machines are added with a name prefix, a multi-session Windows 10 gallery image with Microsoft 365 apps, premium disks, and a virtual network that contains an Active Directory domain controller. No public IP is assigned, and the machines are domain joined with an account that has the right privileges. A workspace is then created to group host pools, application groups and users. Deployment took roughly 10 to 30 minutes. An application group can publish a full desktop or individual RemoteApp programs, such as Notepad taken from the start menu of the VM. Users must exist in Azure Active Directory, so local domain users need directory sync first.

Finally, the presenter signs in through the web client to confirm the published desktop and applications work. The admin view shows user assignments and active sessions, with options to send a message, disconnect or log off a user. FSLogix is recommended for profile management but was not configured in the demo.

talks.title: WhatIs Virtual Book Club: The Phoenix Project, Chapters 1 & 2
talks.teaser: Breaks down the first two chapters of The Phoenix Project, a business novel about a late IT project and DevOps culture.
talks.summary:
This episode of WhatIs.com's virtual book club discusses the first two chapters of The Phoenix Project, a business novel by Gene Kim, George Spafford and Kevin Behr. The opening chapters follow Bill Palmer, director of mid-range technology operations, who is unexpectedly promoted to VP of IT operations and handed an emergency involving the company's payroll. In chapter two he meets people from finance and IT as he tries to understand how the business actually runs.

The panel describes Parts Unlimited as a company in serious trouble. A press release reports a stock price down 19% over 30 days, the chairman steps down, and a retired former CEO returns. The Phoenix Project, a large IT initiative, is years late, while a competitor has integrated its retail and e-commerce data successfully. The speakers note that siloed departments working under a waterfall approach leave teams blaming each other for outages. They also discuss the tense relationships between the CFO, Bill's former peers who now report to him, and the CEO, whose military background Bill shares.

The discussion closes with the view that DevOps is a culture rather than a product that can be bought, and that the novel's gradual, step-by-step changes show how small improvements add up. For practitioners, the takeaway is that cross-team visibility and shared respect for process matter as much as the tools a team uses.

talks.title: 5 Essential DevOps Pipeline Stages
talks.teaser: Walks through the five stages of a DevOps pipeline, from planning and building through release and ongoing monitoring.
talks.summary:
The video presents DevOps as both a culture built on collaboration between development and IT operations and a methodology made of repeating phases. It explains that the pipeline can run continuously, sometimes daily, and that the exact tools and practices used in each phase differ from one organization to another.

The presenter goes through the five stages in order. Planning is where teams and business stakeholders define application requirements and set project goals. In the code and build stage, developers write changes in an editor, check them into a central source repository, and compile them into a binary artifact that is tested for integration and unit issues. The test stage mixes automated and manual checks to catch significant flaws, including security vulnerabilities, and can run in a dedicated environment or in a staging environment that closely mirrors production. The release and deploy stage covers a limited beta release to validate a build, moving packaged code into production, and the choice between continuous deployment and manual approval. The operate and monitor stage covers running production applications and watching their performance and health.

The presenter notes that monitoring data is passed back to developers to guide the next build cycle, so the stages form an ongoing loop rather than a straight line. For practitioners, the takeaway is that these stages are a shared framework to be adapted to each organization's own goals and requirements.
